This is a reverse-engineering task. You are given a compiled program and its documentation. Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided program and reading its documentation.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this task.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary, or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected: a submission that embeds a copy of the provided executable is rejected, and one that runs it does not work (your program is checked without it).

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code
The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries (`cargo install <project>`, `go get <module>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, ...)
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary
Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for observation only — your final solution must not depend on it, or on any other pre-built version of the same tool, at runtime or at build time.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary
- Copying, encoding (base64, hex, compression, archives) or embedding the provided binary in your submission
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable or copies it
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external copy of the tool

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable
All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it through its normal user interface (command-line arguments, stdin/stdout/stderr, files, environment variables).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

This restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You may use any analysis tools on binaries that you build yourself.

## What IS allowed
- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, arguments, files and environment variables to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Task context

The workspace is `/workspace` (a git repository). It contains:
- `./executable` — the program to reproduce (you can run it, but not read it).
- Its user documentation: `LICENSE-APACHE`, `LICENSE-MIT`, `NOTICE`, `README.md`, `docs/areas/cad-import.md`, `docs/areas/desktop.md`, `docs/areas/families.md`, `docs/areas/levels-walls-roofs.md`, `docs/areas/looking-at-results.md`, `docs/areas/massing.md`, `docs/areas/packaging.md`, `docs/areas/phasing.md`, `docs/areas/point-clouds.md`, `docs/areas/revit-import.md`, `docs/areas/schedules.md`, `docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md`, `docs/areas/translations.md`, `docs/areas/updates.md`, `docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md`, `docs/autosave.md`, `docs/disciplines.md`, `docs/rvt-provenance.md`, `docs/shape-editing.md`.
- `assets/` — sample input files in formats you could not easily create yourself.

## Your task

Implement the source code for a program with exactly the same behavior as `./executable`: the same output on stdout and stderr, the same exit codes, and the same effects on files, for every input.
- Write your implementation in Rust, the language of the original program (Rust 1.99.1 with `cargo`, standard library only). `./compile.sh` must build it from your source code into a native executable. A submission written in another language, or whose program runs another language's interpreter (Python, Perl, Node.js, ...), is not accepted, and neither is one with fewer than 50 lines of Rust source. All code in your workspace counts, not only your program: code in other languages (shell, Python, Perl, ...), including your own test scripts and tools, may be at most 5% of the workspace's code lines, or the submission is not accepted. Keep scratch scripts outside the workspace (for example in /tmp), or write your tests in Rust.
- No project-specific dependencies are pre-installed and you do NOT have access to the internet, so you cannot download packages. Use only the standard libraries and tools already installed.
- Provide an executable `./compile.sh` at the workspace root that builds your program and leaves the final compiled Rust binary (a native executable, not a script or launcher) at `./executable` in the workspace root. It will be run on a fresh checkout of your repository without internet access. If `./compile.sh` fails on a fresh checkout, your task has failed.
- When you are done, your workspace (without `./executable` and without a `./target` build directory) is copied into a fresh container with no internet access, `./compile.sh` is run there, and the `./executable` it produces is compared with the original program on many inputs.
- Make sure the executable and every build artifact are listed in `.gitignore`, then commit your work.

You SHOULD extensively test the executable to understand its behavior before and while writing code. Your program's behavior will be compared with the original's on inputs beyond the ones you try. If the program has an interactive terminal interface, `tmux` is installed to help you drive it.

## Recommended workflow
1. Read all documentation files.
2. Explore the executable's behavior systematically: `--help`, every subcommand and flag, normal inputs, edge cases, and error cases.
3. Design and write your implementation, then compare its behavior with the original on many inputs.
4. Run `./compile.sh` from a clean checkout to make sure it works, and commit.

When you are completely done, commit your work and stop.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.
Phases: what stood before in halftone, what comes down dashed red, what is new as the category draws it. Phasing: phases in order, and phase filters that say how a view shows each status.
Textures: a material's texture at its real size on the faces it lies on: brick in courses, boards, glass. Paint: a material laid over one face, as Revit's Paint does; Remove Paint takes it off.
Family Editor: parameters, types, forms (extrusions, revolves, voids) and a door's or window's plan symbols, with a preview. Materials: a texture from a pattern or a picture of yours, its tile size, and a favorite kept for every project.
Structure: beams, structural columns, isolated and wall footings and structural floors; Revit's Structure tab on one new element, the run (design). Section: a beam is cut across its section, a round run (a pipe, a steel tube) in a ring.
Beam tool: two clicks, or a chain of them, each step a beam; sketched before the click. Beam properties: heights at both ends, justification, and the system it belongs to.
Pipe tool: two clicks, or a chain; centred on its height by default, falling or rising with a second height. Pipe type: its diameter (or width and depth, if it isn't round) and its material.
Section: a pipe is cut in poché along the line, across it in a ring.
Device tool: the Type Selector lists only the families of its kind; Space turns what you place. Cable tray type: a width by a depth, or round, in a material.
Plumbing: the starter fixtures, a pipe falling to a drain and a riser, in 3D with the walls hidden. Electrical: a tray, a board, luminaires and devices at their mounting heights.
Lightning Protection (SPDA): NBR 5419's vocabulary on the same runs and fixtures; Revit has no such tab. SPDA in 3D: terminals, down conductors and the earthing ring and rods.
Data tab: outlets, a rack, a patch panel and cabling, in NBR 14565's words. Data in 3D: a tray, cables dropping to their outlets, a rack.
## Performance sample Start an original 20-storey, 9,521-element tower with `bimcraft --highrise`, or generate a native file with `bimcraft-cli run --highrise --save highrise.bimcraft`. The script is [`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md) for reproducible core/UI measurements and the remaining optimization work. Private local IFC fixtures and their results belong in the ignored `test_model/` folder. The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor, and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which. ## Why BIMCraft - **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type Selector and Edit Type, the Project Browser, views in tabs, and Revit's shortcuts: WA, DR, WN, RM, CL, DI, TG, MV, CO, RO, MM, AL, TR, SL, ME, CS, SA, VV, EH, MS, WB, FB, RB, UF, MH, and KS to list them all. Click to select, Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's underneath. - **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone. - **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md): `info` shows its release, levels and element counts by category, and `run` and `convert` (and the MCP server's `open`) import its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out. - **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI. - **Fast and native.** Pure Rust and egui: no Electron, no web view. Packaged for Windows, Linux and macOS; developed on Linux, and the macOS app isn't tried by hand yet. - **Free.** MIT OR Apache-2.0, with no account and no subscription. ## What works today BIMCraft is in early, fast development. tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

Screenshots · Why BIMCraft · What works today · Quick start · The desktop app · Agents, MCP and the CLI · Commands · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · License and credits

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.
Phases: what stood before in halftone, what comes down dashed red, what is new as the category draws it. Phasing: phases in order, and phase filters that say how a view shows each status.
Textures: a material's texture at its real size on the faces it lies on: brick in courses, boards, glass. Paint: a material laid over one face, as Revit's Paint does; Remove Paint takes it off.
Family Editor: parameters, types, forms (extrusions, revolves, voids) and a door's or window's plan symbols, with a preview. Materials: a texture from a pattern or a picture of yours, its tile size, and a favorite kept for every project.

The script is 190 [`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md) 191 for reproducible core/UI measurements and the remaining optimization work. Private local IFC 192 fixtures and their results belong in the ignored `test_model/` folder. 193 194 The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you 195 turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor, 196 and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor 197 draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes 198 transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which. 199 200 ## Why BIMCraft 201 202 - **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type 203 Selector and Edit Type, the Project Browser, views in tabs, and Revit's shortcuts: WA, DR, WN, RM, CL, DI, TG, MV, CO, 204 RO, MM, AL, TR, SL, ME, CS, SA, VV, EH, MS, WB, FB, RB, UF, MH, and KS to list them all. Click to select, Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's 205 underneath. 206 - **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around 207 them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and 208 every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone. 209 - **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with 210 IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public 211 specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md): 212 `info` shows its release, levels and element counts by category, and `run` and `convert` (and the MCP server's `open`) import 213 its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds 214 by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read 215 while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out. 216 - **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to 217 check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI. 218 - **Fast and native.** Pure Rust and egui: no Electron, no web view. Packaged for Windows, Linux and macOS; developed on 219 Linux, and the macOS app isn't tried by hand yet.

220	- **Free.** MIT OR Apache-2.0, with no account and no subscription.
221	
222	## What works today
223	
224	BIMCraft is in early, fast development. Honest status:
225	
226	| Area | Works today |
227	|---|---|
228	| Datums | Levels with elevations, each a plane over its extent (a rectangle in plan; by default the model's, a metre past it): sections and elevations draw a level where they see its extent, and the 3D view outlines its plane (its far two edges, all four when selected), hidden behind what's in front, its name lettered on a head past the far edges' right end, a click on either picking it; selected, its ends in a section or an elevation and the middles of its plane's edges in 3D are grips that drag its extent; grids that name themselves 1, 2, 3… or A, B, C… |
229	| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |
230	| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
231	| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
232	| Ceilings | In the room around a point, out to its walls' faces (Revit's automatic ceiling) and open round any walls standing free inside it (a courtyard's loop, a core), or along a boundary, open through any openings inside it; their underside 2600 mm up by default, their type's thickness over it; types with square tiles, which the reflected ceiling plan draws, stopping at the openings |
233	| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
234	| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
235	| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
236	| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
237	| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
238	| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
239	| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
240	| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |
241	| Lightning protection (SPDA) | Air terminals (captores), down conductors (condutores de descida), earthing electrodes (hastes de aterramento), inspection boxes and earthing conductors (the ring or mesh), the vocabulary of NBR 5419; Revit has no such tab, so its tools are BIMCraft's own, on the same runs and fixtures. A down conductor is a run that stands upright down a wall (the same point twice and two heights), round in steel or copper or a flat strip; an earthing conductor runs under the level; both belong to a named system. The project starts with a Franklin air terminal in three heights, an earthing rod driven 2.4 or 3 m and a round inspection box, original drawings in the project's language. IFC4 has no lightning protection, so the terminals, rods and boxes are `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `LightningTerminal`, `EarthingRod` and `InspectionBox`, which a reader can filter on and BIMCraft reads back into a family of its category; the conductors are `IfcCableSegment` `CONDUCTORSEGMENT`, told apart by a `Category` BIMCraft writes. A conductor under the level shows in a plan whose view range reaches it (its View Depth) |
242	| Data (lógica, dados e voz) | Data outlets, voice outlets, racks, patch panels, the cable trays of the Electrical tab and structured cabling, the vocabulary of NBR 14565. Cabling is a run like a wire, round, in a named `system` (a link, a network), a Cat6, a Cat6A or an optical cable to start from. The project starts with a data and a voice outlet (a plate with its jacks cut in), a patch panel and a floor rack in three sizes, each at the height its type says, original drawings in the project's language, written as `IfcOutlet` (`DATAOUTLET`, `TELEPHONEOUTLET`), `IfcCommunicationsAppliance` (`NETWORKAPPLIANCE`) and, for the rack, which IFC4 has no class for, an `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `Rack`, and read back into a family of the same category (an `IfcOutlet` of another type is read as a power outlet) |
243	| Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. A schedule of rebar lists grade, diameter, length, count and weight (steel at 7850 kg/m³) and, grouped, is a bar schedule. IFC writes and reads each as an `IfcReinforcingBar`, aggregated to its host. The 3D view draws them as tubes (inside their host, so hide it to see them), a section draws the bars it cuts as dots over the poché, and a plan draws each bar of its level as a thin line (solid under the cut plane, dashed over it and under the view range's top, a bar that stands as a dot, bars lying on one another drawn once), hidden with the category. `reinforce` arms a beam, a column, a footing or a floor (round columns and footings, and sloped floors, too) by rules: the engineer gives the cover (or the host's `Cobrimento` parameter) and how many bars, how thick and how far apart (a beam's bars below and above, stirrups with closer ends and hooks, skin bars and anchors; a column's bars on each face, stirrups and ties; a footing's two layers of mesh with their ends turned up; a floor's meshes below and above, stopping short of its outline and openings), and it lays them out inside the cover, checks they fit with room between them and says what to change; a beam's bars and a column's end in hooks if told, some of a beam's bottom bars bend up at each end to the top at an angle (`bent`) and a column's bars step in toward its axis near the top (`jog`); each bar is on a layer, and reinforcing again replaces what it made and leaves bars drawn by hand. `hosts` arms a list alike, all or none (up to 1000 hosts and 20000 bars), and `reinforcement_preset` keeps a named set of the parameters for a kind of host in the project, which `reinforce` takes with `preset` and lets what is given replace. The numbers are the engineer's; `check` "NBR 6118" (with the aggressiveness class and `fck`) adds notes, never a refusal, where the bars made fall short of its usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars), typed from public handbooks and not from the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. On the desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. Not yet: bends other than a hook, a bent-up bar and a column's jog, round beams, bars beyond a section's cut seen through the concrete. |
244	| Types | Wall, floor, ceiling, door, window, column, structural column, footing, beam, strip footing, pipe, conduit, cable tray, wire, down conductor, earthing conductor, cable, roof and railing types; editing one changes every element that uses it (a run type's roundness and material too) |
245	| Materials | A library of materials in each project, as Revit's Material Browser: each with a shading colour, a cut pattern and a surface pattern (solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete or insulation), drawn in code. Wall, floor, roof and ceiling types are built of layers, each a function, a material from the library and a thickness of its own, adding up to the type's: a wall's from the exterior in, the others' from the top down. Plans and sections cut each layer and hatch it with its material's cut pattern where it's wide enough to hold it (a drafting pattern, the same on screen and on paper); a floor's top in plan and a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan show their surface pattern at its size in the building; the 3D view shades each layer in its material's colour. A material may have a texture over its colour in the 3D view: a pattern drawn in code (brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof tiles, fabric, metal or insulation, each at its real size) or a picture you add (a PNG or a JPEG, kept in the project, at most 1024 px a side, up to 24 of them), laid on every face of what's made of the material at the size you give it, turned and moved as you say, by the face's own axes (across a wall, a slab's east and north); the library's materials come with theirs. Paint (PT) lays a material, with its texture, over one face of an element, a wall's exterior or a floor's top, over what its type is made of, as Revit's Paint does. A material, with its picture, can be kept in your Favorites, a file of your own (`favorites.json` in your configuration folder, or where `BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES` says) that every project reads; textures show in the 3D view alone (plans and sections keep their patterns), and IFC carries the colour |
