an `IfcSystem` of its name, stairs and ramps as their flights, landings and railings (each railing with its rail's top line as its axis), roofs as closed shells of flat faces (hip, gable, shed or flat), openings that cut the walls and hold the doors and windows, an opening for each slab, ceiling and roof a shaft passes through, masses as building element proxies of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set), and components as furniture, sanitary or waste terminals, pipe fittings, valves, distribution boards, outlets, switching devices, communications appliances, light fixtures or proxies, named `Family:Type` as Revit names them, each form a closed face set in its material's colour, each element's values of the project parameters in a `Project Parameters` property set (dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations belong to views, and stay out of it), and each element's phase and design option in a `BIMCraft_Phasing` property set: its `Phase Created` is always named in it, the first phase too (said to be implied, for another tool to read; a door or window says only what it holds, as one with no phase follows its wall), `Phase Demolished` and `Design Option` where it holds them, and the project's phases in order, with the phase filters, overrides and option sets it changed, in one on the project, and, as IFC says it, its `Status` in its `Pset_*Common` (`EXISTING`, `DEMOLISH`, `NEW` or `TEMPORARY`, for another tool to filter the work by); a project that uses none of it writes none |
264	| Agents | MCP server, scripts, and every command callable with JSON |
265	| Desktop | Revit's layout: ribbon tabs with a contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type Selector and Type Properties, the Project Browser and views in tabs; a plan and a reflected ceiling plan per level that pan and zoom, sections and elevations, a 3D view that orbits, and sheets; tools for walls (straight or arcs, on the location line picked), doors, windows, columns, roofs by footprint (and Gable Edge, to stand a roof's edge upright) and by extrusion, dormers, floors (and a floor's slope arrow), ceilings, shaft openings, sketch mode (Edit Boundary on a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft, and Boundary Line or Sketch Ceiling for a new one: lines, rectangles, arcs and Pick Walls, sketch lines with ids of their own picked by click or box and moved by their grips, Finish Edit Mode saying what's wrong and marking the lines; in the 3D view, Edit Boundary sketches on the element's own plane, and Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft sketch on the view's Work Plane: a level from the list, a surface or three points picked on the model (snapping to corners), each with an offset, at any angle; walls, beams and braces, columns and structural columns, footings, pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays and components draw in the 3D view on the level face under the cursor, snapping as a plan does, a run climbing from one face to another; they need it horizontal), masses (and floors, walls and roofs from them), stairs and ramps (run by run, turning at landings), railings, rooms, levels, grids, dimensions (aligned, angular, radial), spot elevations, text, detail lines, filled and masking regions, tags, sections and elevations; Flip, Attach Top/Base and Detach Top/Base for walls; a wall, floor, roof or ceiling type's layers in Type Properties, and the project's materials in Manage > Materials; project parameters in Manage > Project Parameters, and their values in Properties; schedules from View > Schedules, their fields, filters, sorting and totals in Schedule Properties; the Component tool, families and their types in the Type Selector, the Project Browser and Type Properties, a component's own parameters in Properties, and Load Family; Crop View with grips to drag a crop region's edges, and the view range in Properties; project units, metric or feet and inches; Revit's selection (click, Ctrl, Shift, Tab, window and crossing boxes); dragging and the Modify panel (Align, Offset, Mirror, Split, Move, Copy, Rotate, Trim/Extend to Corner) and its Phasing panel (Demolish); Paint and Remove Paint on its Geometry panel, for the 3D view; typed lengths and temporary dimensions; undo and redo; open, save and export; a light and a dark theme; English, Portuguese or Spanish. The Manage tab has the Materials window (with textures and pictures), the Favorites, Object Styles, Annotation Settings (Line Weights, Line Styles, Line Patterns and Fill Patterns, a fill pattern simple or made of detail lines picked in a plan and the tile between two corners), and the Family Editor (New Family, Edit Family) |
266	| Updates | The desktop app asks GitHub for the latest release when it starts, on a thread of its own, so it never delays the start, and says so in a banner when one is newer: Update now, Later or Skip this version. Update now downloads the new version and checks its SHA-256 against the digest GitHub lists for it; Restart and install then asks to save, closes, replaces the program in place and starts again with the same project. That works for the copy the Windows installer made, an AppImage and the macOS app, where you can write to their folder. Any other copy (a package from your distribution, a tarball, a build from source) gets a Download button for the release's page, and a Flatpak, which has no network, never checks. File > Check for updates at startup switches the check off, and `BIMCRAFT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` keeps the app from making any request. `bimcraft-cli` and the MCP server never phone home; see [Updates](#updates) for what the check does and doesn't protect against, and for what has run on which system |
267	
268	The export writes one type object for each type its walls, slabs, beams, columns, footings, doors, windows, roofs, ceilings, components and runs use (`IfcWallType`, `IfcSlabType`, `IfcBeamType`, `IfcColumnType`, `IfcFootingType`, `IfcDoorType`, `IfcWindowType`, `IfcRoofType`, `IfcCoveringType`, the class each component is written as, and `IfcPipeSegmentType`, `IfcDuctSegmentType`, `IfcCableCarrierSegmentType` and `IfcCableSegmentType`), related to its occurrences by `IfcRelDefinesByType`; strip footings have none yet. Beams and columns carry `Qto_BeamBaseQuantities` and `Qto_ColumnBaseQuantities`.
269	
270	The IFC4 export is checked with [IfcOpenShell](https://ifcopenshell.org) 0.9: the sample house has no schema or EXPRESS rule
271	errors, every element builds its geometry, and the walls' volumes (with the openings cut out), the roof's and the slabs' and
272	ceilings' (with their shafts cut out) match a hand calculation, as do the roofs' of an L-shaped house with a dormer and an
273	extrusion roof beside it, and of houses round a courtyard, their floors and ceilings open over it too, and of a house of
274	layered walls, floors, ceilings and roofs, each with its material layer set, and of a flat furnished from the library, a
275	mirrored chair among it. Import is checked against it too: the sample comes back the same from IFC, element by element, also with its
276	geometry turned into triangle meshes by IfcOpenShell, and a building IfcOpenShell's API writes comes in whole, its roofs
277	(slabs per slope, round a courtyard too, or a profile extruded) and its floors and ceilings round a courtyard (a profile with
278	a void, or a mesh) among it, and its walls' and slabs' layers on the faces their layer sets are stacked from, and its furniture (a stool type placed
279	twice, one turned, a proxy, a meshed basin) as components where it stood. Project parameters go out as property sets IfcOpenShell
280	reads back typed as they were (text, a real, a length, a boolean), and come in from a property set its API writes, in metres. A phased sample has no schema or EXPRESS rule errors either, and
281	IfcOpenShell reads each element's `BIMCraft_Phasing` set and the project's list of phases; they come back from IFC as they went
282	out, and from a set its API writes (labels and a list value), while a set another tool calls its own, `Phasing` say, is left unread.
283	
284	## Quick start
285	
286	The engine and the CLI need Rust 1.90 or later; the desktop app needs 1.95 (egui 0.36).
287	
288	```sh
289	git clone https://github.com/IPedrax/bimcraft
290	cd bimcraft
291	cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample       # opens the sample house
292	```
293	
294	Without a window:
295	
296	```sh
297	cargo build --release
298	./target/release/bimcraft-cli run --sample --save house.bimcraft --save house.ifc --save plan.png
299	```

file.content:
- **Free.** MIT OR Apache-2.0, with no account and no subscription.

## What works today

BIMCraft is in early, fast development. Honest status:

| Area | Works today |
|---|---|
| Datums | Levels with elevations, each a plane over its extent (a rectangle in plan; by default the model's, a metre past it): sections and elevations draw a level where they see its extent, and the 3D view outlines its plane (its far two edges, all four when selected), hidden behind what's in front, its name lettered on a head past the far edges' right end, a click on either picking it; selected, its ends in a section or an elevation and the middles of its plane's edges in 3D are grips that drag its extent; grids that name themselves 1, 2, 3… or A, B, C… |
| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |
| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
| Ceilings | In the room around a point, out to its walls' faces (Revit's automatic ceiling) and open round any walls standing free inside it (a courtyard's loop, a core), or along a boundary, open through any openings inside it; their underside 2600 mm up by default, their type's thickness over it; types with square tiles, which the reflected ceiling plan draws, stopping at the openings |
| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |
| Lightning protection (SPDA) | Air terminals (captores), down conductors (condutores de descida), earthing electrodes (hastes de aterramento), inspection boxes and earthing conductors (the ring or mesh), the vocabulary of NBR 5419; Revit has no such tab, so its tools are BIMCraft's own, on the same runs and fixtures. A down conductor is a run that stands upright down a wall (the same point twice and two heights), round in steel or copper or a flat strip; an earthing conductor runs under the level; both belong to a named system. The project starts with a Franklin air terminal in three heights, an earthing rod driven 2.4 or 3 m and a round inspection box, original drawings in the project's language. IFC4 has no lightning protection, so the terminals, rods and boxes are `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `LightningTerminal`, `EarthingRod` and `InspectionBox`, which a reader can filter on and BIMCraft reads back into a family of its category; the conductors are `IfcCableSegment` `CONDUCTORSEGMENT`, told apart by a `Category` BIMCraft writes. A conductor under the level shows in a plan whose view range reaches it (its View Depth) |
| Data (lógica, dados e voz) | Data outlets, voice outlets, racks, patch panels, the cable trays of the Electrical tab and structured cabling, the vocabulary of NBR 14565. Cabling is a run like a wire, round, in a named `system` (a link, a network), a Cat6, a Cat6A or an optical cable to start from. The project starts with a data and a voice outlet (a plate with its jacks cut in), a patch panel and a floor rack in three sizes, each at the height its type says, original drawings in the project's language, written as `IfcOutlet` (`DATAOUTLET`, `TELEPHONEOUTLET`), `IfcCommunicationsAppliance` (`NETWORKAPPLIANCE`) and, for the rack, which IFC4 has no class for, an `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `Rack`, and read back into a family of the same category (an `IfcOutlet` of another type is read as a power outlet) |
| Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. A schedule of rebar lists grade, diameter, length, count and weight (steel at 7850 kg/m³) and, grouped, is a bar schedule. IFC writes and reads each as an `IfcReinforcingBar`, aggregated to its host. The 3D view draws them as tubes (inside their host, so hide it to see them), a section draws the bars it cuts as dots over the poché, and a plan draws each bar of its level as a thin line (solid under the cut plane, dashed over it and under the view range's top, a bar that stands as a dot, bars lying on one another drawn once), hidden with the category. `reinforce` arms a beam, a column, a footing or a floor (round columns and footings, and sloped floors, too) by rules: the engineer gives the cover (or the host's `Cobrimento` parameter) and how many bars, how thick and how far apart (a beam's bars below and above, stirrups with closer ends and hooks, skin bars and anchors; a column's bars on each face, stirrups and ties; a footing's two layers of mesh with their ends turned up; a floor's meshes below and above, stopping short of its outline and openings), and it lays them out inside the cover, checks they fit with room between them and says what to change; a beam's bars and a column's end in hooks if told, some of a beam's bottom bars bend up at each end to the top at an angle (`bent`) and a column's bars step in toward its axis near the top (`jog`); each bar is on a layer, and reinforcing again replaces what it made and leaves bars drawn by hand. `hosts` arms a list alike, all or none (up to 1000 hosts and 20000 bars), and `reinforcement_preset` keeps a named set of the parameters for a kind of host in the project, which `reinforce` takes with `preset` and lets what is given replace. The numbers are the engineer's; `check` "NBR 6118" (with the aggressiveness class and `fck`) adds notes, never a refusal, where the bars made fall short of its usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars), typed from public handbooks and not from the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. On the desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. Not yet: bends other than a hook, a bent-up bar and a column's jog, round beams, bars beyond a section's cut seen through the concrete. |
| Types | Wall, floor, ceiling, door, window, column, structural column, footing, beam, strip footing, pipe, conduit, cable tray, wire, down conductor, earthing conductor, cable, roof and railing types; editing one changes every element that uses it (a run type's roundness and material too) |
| Materials | A library of materials in each project, as Revit's Material Browser: each with a shading colour, a cut pattern and a surface pattern (solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete or insulation), drawn in code. Wall, floor, roof and ceiling types are built of layers, each a function, a material from the library and a thickness of its own, adding up to the type's: a wall's from the exterior in, the others' from the top down. Plans and sections cut each layer and hatch it with its material's cut pattern where it's wide enough to hold it (a drafting pattern, the same on screen and on paper); a floor's top in plan and a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan show their surface pattern at its size in the building; the 3D view shades each layer in its material's colour. A material may have a texture over its colour in the 3D view: a pattern drawn in code (brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof tiles, fabric, metal or insulation, each at its real size) or a picture you add (a PNG or a JPEG, kept in the project, at most 1024 px a side, up to 24 of them), laid on every face of what's made of the material at the size you give it, turned and moved as you say, by the face's own axes (across a wall, a slab's east and north); the library's materials come with theirs. Paint (PT) lays a material, with its texture, over one face of an element, a wall's exterior or a floor's top, over what its type is made of, as Revit's Paint does. A material, with its picture, can be kept in your Favorites, a file of your own (`favorites.json` in your configuration folder, or where `BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES` says) that every project reads; textures show in the 3D view alone (plans and sections keep their patterns), and IFC carries the colour |
| Editing | Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is); move, copy, rotate and mirror, with the walls joined to them stretching to stay joined and doors and windows going with their walls (a mirrored wall runs back the other way, its exterior mirrored); trim or extend two walls to a corner; split a wall, an arc into two arcs; flip walls; delete (a wall takes its doors and windows with it, and they their tags; a roof or floor walls are attached to lets them go); undo and redo |
| Snaps and the ruler | Points picked while drawing stick to what the plan has there, as Revit's snaps do: the ends, middles and centres of walls (an arc's too), grids and components, the centres of columns, structural columns and footings with the corners and edge middles of their outlines (a round one's four quadrants), so a wall can start flush with a column's edge, and the corners of floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; where two straight walls or grids cross; the foot of the perpendicular from the last point to a straight wall or grid; and a wall's centre line, so a wall drawn onto it meets it. It also sticks to the anchors of notes, dimensions, tags, spot elevations, section and elevation marks, detail groups and repeating details; a camera's mark gives its eye and target, never the body, lens or name it is drawn with. Each shows its own marker and its name. A direction from the last point sticks to multiples of an angle (5°, 15°, 30°, 45° or 90°; 15° by default), from east and from the line before it, so corners come out exact, sharp ones too: a dashed guide shows it, and where it crosses a wall or grid the point lands there. The line being drawn carries a ruler: graduations at round lengths, its length and its angle (at the corner it turns once there's a line before it, drawn as an arc). Manage > Snaps switches each snap and sets the angle steps, and Revit's SE, SM, SI, SC, SP and SN take one snap alone for the next point (SO none, SS back); Measure (ME) lays a ruler between two snapped points and reads its length, parts and angle; the `measure` command does the same. Each plan, section and elevation has a background grid, a main grid and a subgrid with their own spacing, divisions, colours and pens, turned by an angle, kept in the view's graphics and controlled by its template; Grid snapping (Manage > Snaps, or the grid menu in the view control bar) lands a free point on its crossings |
| Annotation | Aligned dimensions between parallel references, one segment or a chain: wall faces, centre lines and ends, door and window centres and jambs, grids; and between endpoints (a wall's ends and its faces' corners, a line's or a grid's ends, a jamb's), aligned along them or linear, horizontal or vertical, as the cursor lies or the Options Bar says (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them); angular dimensions between two lines that meet, radial and diameter ones on round columns, curved walls, circles and arcs, and arc length ones along a curved wall or an arc; all measuring the model as it is, so they follow what they measure (a change that would turn a reference out of parallel with the others is refused). In a 3D view, aligned dimensions between two points or edges of the model (square to an edge), kept by the view and drawn over it, on either painter and on the sheets that hold it. A dimension's number takes a typed length and moves what it measures; locked segments show their padlocks always; Align leaves a padlock that keeps the two lines aligned after every change, refusing one the other locks can't hold with. Dimension types, as Revit's type parameters: continuous, baseline or ordinate strings, diagonal, arrow, open arrow or dot ticks, pens, colour, the dimension and witness lines' extensions, gaps and control, and the numbers' font, size, lettering, offset, background, read convention, units and rounding; a dimension's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display (EQ). Tags on any element showing its type, a door's or window's mark, a room's name or any field of its schedule, going where their doors and windows go, with or without a leader; tag everything not tagged yet in one go. Text notes in plans, sections, elevations and on sheets, at any angle, over several lines, with a leader, of a text type (font, size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, colour and a border: any font the system has, Arial by default, which a look-alike such as Liberation Sans stands in for where it isn't installed, or IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono or our single-stroke lettering; any script a font on the system has, CJK included), written and rewritten on the canvas (Shift+Enter breaks a line), and with Override Formatting, parts of them bold, italic or underlined whatever their type; spot elevations reading the top of what they stand on in plan (a floor, a roof's slope, a stair's tread), or the height of a point in a section |
| Views | A floor plan per level with Revit's view range: cut at its cut plane (1200 mm up by default), what lies below seen from it down to the bottom, faint beyond it down to the view depth, and roofs overhead up to the top: wall poché with clean joins at any angle, compound walls' layers, hatched with their materials' cut patterns where they're wide enough (else lighter where they aren't structure), door swings, window glass, room tags, grid bubbles, dimensions, door and window tags; PNG and SVG, which letter the view's name at the plan's bottom left (the window letters it too, over the canvas and on the screen only, which File > Settings can hide; a viewport on a sheet has its own title). Sections and elevations along any line: the cut in poché (a roof's along its slope, a compound wall's, floor's, roof's or ceiling's with its layers), what lies beyond in hidden line, levels named with their heights, grids; the four building elevations in one go; their marks on every plan; PNG. Crop regions on plans and sections: the view shows only what's inside, grids stopping at its edge with their bubbles. A reflected ceiling plan per level: its walls cut at 2300 mm (over the doors, through the windows), looking up at the ceilings, their tiles and the shafts through them, and at the beams and columns over the cut up to the ceilings, in projection (one over a ceiling is hidden by it). A 3D view, from any angle: walls with their doors and windows cut out, slabs and ceilings with their shafts cut out, columns, stairs and roofs, door leaves and glass, shaded (each layer in its material's colour), with an edge wherever faces meet, but none between the facets of a curve (a curved wall's, a round form's, an imported mesh's where its triangles turn less than 20°), which shades smoothly across them; PNG. A plan or a section always has a scale, 1 : n (1 : 100, or 1/8" = 1'-0" in feet and inches, until set): it stands for paper at that scale, and its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, marks, dimension ticks) and its line weights are that paper's, so on screen a line is as thick as it would print at the zoom (at least a pixel; Thin Lines draws all of them one). A line weight is a pen, 1 to 16, or 0, a hairline, the thinnest line the screen, a PNG or a printer draws, at any scale and zoom; what pens 1 to 16 draw is the project's Line Weights (Manage > Line Weights, as Revit's): the model's pens at each of a list of scales, a view taking the nearest scale's, and the annotation's (dimensions, tags, text, grids, levels, marks) at any scale, edited by scale, added and deleted, applied as one undo step and saved with the project. Which pen each model category draws its own lines in, cut and seen, is the project's Object Styles (Manage > Object Styles, as Revit's), in every plan and section, a view's Visibility/Graphics over them. Detail lines draw in one view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet) in a line style: a pen, a colour and a line pattern, its freely ordered gaps, straight strokes, dots, centered parallel offsets, waves, zigzags and text in mm on paper so it reads the same at any scale; the Line Pattern Creator previews straight or curved paths and letters text with bundled IBM Plex Sans, while geometry and dimensions keep the centerline (Manage > Line Styles, styles and patterns made, changed, renamed and deleted as one undo step; a project starts with Thin, Medium and Wide Lines, a Hairline, Hidden, Centre and Overhead Lines). A cut wall's outline is inked over its poché, and not across where walls join. A plan or a section has a detail level too: coarse (what it cuts in one poché, an opening as its gap and jambs), medium (a compound element's layers and an opening's leaf, swing and glass) or fine, as it has always drawn (the layers' patterns too); the 3D view has a visual style: shaded, hidden line (paper-white faces with their edges, what a face hides staying hidden) or wireframe (every edge, seen through the faces). A viewport takes its view's scale; a sheet keeps annotation at paper size. A view fitted into an image (a PNG, Zoom to Fit) leaves as much room round it as its annotation takes at its scale, which grows with the scale, so 1 : 500 doesn't cut its grid bubbles or level names off. A level can have more plans than its own, as Revit's Duplicate View makes them (`duplicate_view`, DP): each a plan view with its own view range, crop and graphics and its own dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations over the same model; with detailing it starts with its source's annotation; a dependent view follows its parent's view range and graphics (scale and detail too), has a crop of its own, and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. They go on sheets, take view templates and have ceiling plans as levels do. Sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet. The 3D view is parallel (axonometric) or in perspective, as through a camera: picked from Projection in its Properties (or `perspective`), seen through a lens of a focal length typed there, from an eye raised or lowered to a height typed there, and orbited, panned, zoomed, picked and edited as ever, on the processor or the graphics card. The Camera tool (`camera`) makes a view of its own, as Revit's does: an eye and a target are clicked in a plan (each at a height over it, typed in the Options Bar), and a named 3D view in perspective opens looking from the eye at the target; it is listed under 3D Views in the Project Browser, opens from its own camera, and its name, eye, target and lens are read and changed in Properties, whether it is open or its mark on the plan is picked (`camera` reads or changes one too, by name or id; a view with no camera shows the azimuth and elevation it is framed by on a sheet instead). The camera shows on its level's plan as a mark at its eye with a line to what it looks at: it is picked there and opened by its right-click menu (or a double click), and its eye and target follow the mouse as the view is orbited, panned or zoomed, so leaving the view and coming back stands it where it was left. The 3D view has a section box, as Revit's: six planes square to the axes that keep what lies between them, the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, turned on and off with BX or its Properties, each face dragged by its grip in the view or typed in Properties, its extents kept while it's off; the levels it doesn't reach are left out. A plan can follow it (Section Box in the plan's Properties): it then shows what the box keeps, cut at the box's top, seen down to its bottom and cropped to its sides, and snaps to a scan where the box's top cuts it |
| Linked models | `link` (LK, Manage > Link Model) shows another project, a BIMCraft file or an IFC, as a reference in this one, as Revit's Link Revit does: what it builds (walls, floors, roofs, ceilings, columns, beams, stairs, railings, pipes and the other runs, components, masses) is drawn halftone in plans, ceiling plans, sections and the 3D view and written into the images, sheets and PDFs, and the picks snap to it. It can't be selected or edited, and the schedules, the checks and the IFC export never see it, so an architect's model is the base to draw the electrical wiring or the plumbing over. It stands origin to origin, moved and turned as the link says (its Origin and Angle in Properties, or `move` and `rotate` on it; it is picked in the Project Browser's Linked Models group, where a right click reloads or removes it); a level of it at the height of one of the project's stands on that one, the others are named after the link. A project keeps the path (relative to its file where it can be) and reads the file again when it opens, saying which links it couldn't read; Reload All, in the right-click menu of the Project Browser's Linked Models, reads them again. A linked project's own links, views, sheets and annotation stay out. Still to come: shared coordinates, per-view visibility and overrides of a link, hosting on a linked wall, and unloading |
| CAD drawings | `import_cad` (Insert > Import CAD, or Link CAD) brings a DXF drawing in, as Revit's Import CAD and Link CAD do: an ASCII DXF of any version, read from the public DXF reference, or a DWG (2000 to 2018), which the desktop and the command line read as DXF through acadrust (MPL-2.0, unmodified), in a process of its own. Its unit comes from the file or is chosen; its middle or its origin goes on the project's origin; it shows the layers its file has on, or all, or those listed; its colours are kept, inverted or black. It is drawn under the model in the plans of its level (or in one plan only), with its layers' colours, line weights and linetypes, text and solid hatches, and the picks snap to its ends, middles, centres and crossings, so walls can be traced over it. It moves, turns and copies as one element; `cad_layers` hides its layers everywhere or in one view (Visibility/Graphics' Imported Categories), `cad_query` names the entity at a point, and a linked one is read again by `reload_cad` and when the project opens. The project keeps the drawing's file, so it opens without it. Still to come: DXF and DWG export, exploding an import, and images and PDFs as underlays |
| Visibility and graphics | What each view hides, and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does, for each plan, section, elevation and 3D view: whole categories left out (walls, doors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels in a section…), or single elements; lines and fills overridden by category, by element and by view filter: a colour, weight and dash for what the view cuts and for what it sees (a plan's below its cut plane, the annotation; in 3D, and in a section beyond its line, the edges' colour), the cut's poché colour or a 3D view's surface colour (a weight is a pen, 0 a hairline at any scale), halftone (halfway to the paper) and, in 3D, transparency, where what lies behind shows through and a click still picks the element (halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can't take its category's away). A hidden door or window leaves its opening in the wall, and snaps, Tag All, Select All and a view's framing take what it shows. View filters pick elements out by rules, a schedule filter's (a field of the category, how to compare it, a value, project parameters among the fields), on the categories chosen; a view applies them in order, the first prevailing where they disagree, and one that hides hides whatever the others say; an element's own override beats the filters', and those beat the category's. View templates keep a view's categories, filters, phase, design options, scale, detail level, visual style and, for a plan, view range under a name, for other views to follow: what a template controls isn't the view's to change, and changed, every view following it follows. A project's filters and templates are saved with it; sheets print each view as its graphics say |
| Phasing and design options | Phases in order, as Revit's Phasing has them (a project starts with Existing and New Construction): each element is made in one (its `Phase Created`, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), so in a view's phase it is new, existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (made and taken down in it), and what is made after the phase, or taken down before it, isn't there. A view has a phase (the project's last unless it says) and a phase filter, which shows each status as its category does, as the project's overrides for that status say (existing in halftone and demolished dashed red to begin with, both yours to change) or not at all; a project starts with Show All, Show Complete, Show New, Show Previous + Demolished and Show Previous + New. A door or window with no phase of its own follows its wall. Phases are added, inserted, renamed and combined, and what was made, taken down or shown in one goes along; phase filters are made and changed. Design options are sets of options, as Revit's Design Options: an element in an option of a set (`Design Option`, `set: option`) shows only in a view that shows that option, the set's primary unless the view chooses, and one in none shows everywhere. Options are added, renamed, made the primary and taken out (one with elements in it stays until they are moved); accepting the primary keeps its elements and takes the others' and the set away, and deleting a set takes its elements too. What a session makes is made in the phase of the view it is drawn in, when that view has a phase or a phase filter of its own, and in the active design option; a copy is made in them too, and isn't taken down with the element it was copied from, while what is made with a phase or an option given keeps it. Schedules and view filters read the phase and the option as fields (a schedule sorts and groups the phases in the project's order, Existing before New Construction, whatever their names; a rule that names a phase, an option or a set follows it when it is renamed or combined); the desktop's Demolish tool (DW) takes an element down in the phase of the view it is clicked in, and a second click takes it back; templates can control a view's phase and its options; sheets print each view in its phase; a project's phases, filters, overrides and sets are saved with it. A project saved before phases that holds a project parameter named `Phase Created`, `Phase Demolished` or `Design Option` opens with it renamed (`Phase Created Parameter`), its values with it |
| Sheets | ISO A0 to A4, landscape, with a title block (project, sheet name and number, scale); plans, sections, elevations and the 3D view placed on them at a scale and titled, schedules as ruled tables, text notes on the paper, a view on one sheet; PNG, and PDF: one sheet, or every sheet a page |
| Schedules | Schedule views of rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, pipes, conduits, cable trays, wires, down conductors, earthing conductors, cables, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, as Revit's Schedule/Quantities makes them: the fields chosen and ordered from the category's own (Area, Width, Count…), the project parameters for it and, for components, their families' parameters; calculated fields, formulas over the row's other fields as a family's are (`Area * 120`, `Perimeter * Finish Height / 1e6`); filters (equals, greater than, contains, begins with, has a value…) that every row holds to, comparing values as the schedule shows them; sorting by fields in turn, ascending or descending (the phase fields in the project's order of phases, not by name), and grouped, a row for each set of their values, its count and totals summed; totals under the rows. Every project has a Room, Door, Window, Wall, Floor and Level Schedule, each the project's own once changed; CSV; on sheets, totals and all |
| Project parameters | Values of your own that each element of their categories holds (text, numbers, lengths, yes or no, unset a no), as Revit's project parameters are: set in Properties or with `modify`, shown, filtered and sorted in schedules and read by their formulas, and written to IFC in a `Project Parameters` property set and read back from it; renamed, schedules follow; taken off a category, its elements and schedules lose them |
| Units | Lengths shown and typed in millimetres, centimetres, metres, fractional inches, decimal feet, or feet and fractional inches (to 1/16"), areas in m² or ft², in drawings, schedules and the desktop alike; a length typed with its own unit (`10' 6 1/2"`, `3 m`) reads as that. The model, files and every command keep millimetres |
| Languages | English, Brazilian Portuguese, Spanish, Czech, French, German, Dutch or Italian for the desktop; those languages or Swedish for each project (and Vietnamese, Simplified or Traditional Chinese for the desktop alone, Chinese drawn with a Chinese font the system has: a drawing's lettering has no hanzi): a project's language names what commands make (levels, sections, elevations, rooms, schedules) and is what its drawings print (SOBE, SUBE, UPP or AUF on stairs, ESCALA, SKALA or MASSSTAB in the title block, schedule headings); what's already named stays. Commands' messages stay English, for agents |
| Families | BIMCraft's own parametric components, never Autodesk's `.rfa`: a family has parameters (lengths, numbers, angles, yes or no, materials; each type's, or each component's), types that set them, and forms, each a profile drawn in its own axes and swept across them, every size a number or a formula as Revit's are (`Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`), each form of a material, there while a yes/no parameter or a formula says. A new project comes with ten of them (tables, chairs, beds, sofas, desks, wardrobes, base cabinets, WCs, washbasins, bathtubs), named and worded in its language; more load from .json files. A component places a family's type at a point, turned and mirrored, its instance parameters its own; plans show it from above, the parts under a higher one hidden (a table's legs under its top), and sections and elevations beyond their line, never cut, as Revit shows furniture; the 3D view shades each form in its material's colour, textured as its material is. A form may be turned about an axis in its plane (a pipe, a bowl, a shade: `axis`, and `from` and `to` in degrees, up to a full turn), and a `void` form cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through (a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, a sash round its pane), exactly: a solid cut by a solid, in any shape. The Family Editor in the desktop edits a family's parameters, types, forms and symbols as text, shows it on a preview you can turn, and makes it the project's, saves it to a `.json` file, or keeps it, with the materials it's made of, in the Favorites |
| IFC import | IFC2x3 and IFC4 files, as Revit and other BIM tools write them: storeys, straight and curved walls with their doors and windows (cut to a roof over them, attached to it), floors level or sloped and ceilings, with the holes in them, rooms, columns (structural ones, which carry load, in their own category), beams, strip footings, pipes, conduits, cable trays, wires, conductors and cables (runs, found as the longest direction a body spreads in and the section square to it, or, when the body is one profile extruded along anything but up, that way, so a beam shorter than it is deep is still a beam; an upright one running up, with the justification and the `IfcSystem` BIMCraft wrote), isolated footings, structural floors, grids, stairs and ramps of straight flights with the landings between them (a landing slab on its own is a floor), railings (by their axis, or a straight one by its body), roofs flat, sloping all round over any footprint with gable ends, courtyards and openings through them, or one profile swept across, masses (proxies of object type `Mass`, a lofted one with its `BIMCraft_Mass` property set), and the openings through floors, ceilings and roofs (as shafts), each measured from its geometry, whether the file extrudes a profile, writes a Brep or a triangle mesh; material layer sets as their types' layers, stacked from the face the file says, with each material's colour; furniture, sanitary and waste terminals, pipe fittings, valves, distribution boards, outlets (power, data and telephone), switching devices, communications appliances, light fixtures and proxies (a lightning terminal, an earthing rod, an inspection box or a rack by its object type) as components of families made of their bodies, a family of the category its class says, a family for each family the file names, a type for each type, and a mirror image of a type that type mirrored; project parameters from a `Project Parameters` property set, each of the kind its values are, and from the single values of any other program's property sets (Eberick's `AltoQi_Eberick_*`, `Pset_ConcreteElementGeneral`, `Pset_BeamCommon`), each named for its property, less the characters a formula can't say, with a beam's, column's, footing's or floor's name, where it isn't its type's, as its Mark (V1, P1, L1); phases and design options from a `BIMCraft_Phasing` property set (the project's phases, phase filters, overrides and option sets from the one on the project, each element's phase and option from its own; what the project can't have is left out and listed, and the element stays); walls that nearly meet are joined; a model at map coordinates is moved near the origin; what can't come in is listed, with why |
| Revit files (read only; the command line and the desktop) | A Revit `.rvt` or `.rfa` file of release 2015 to 2027 (checked on Autodesk's sample projects of 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, and the Snowdon Towers files) is read by a reader of its own, `crates/rvt`, ported in part from [rvt-rs](https://github.com/DrunkOnJava/rvt-rs) and fenced by [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md). `info` shows its release, build and document GUID, the last save (the saver's name when worksharing records it, and the path it was saved to; shown by `info`, never written into a project or an IFC file), the title, the levels with their names and elevations, and the number of elements in each `BuiltInCategory`, how many of them are placed instances. `run x.rvt`, `convert x.rvt out.ifc` and the MCP server's `open` import the file as a new project: its levels, straight and curved walls with their compound layers and materials (the exterior on the side the file's flip says), floors and ceilings from their sketches (holes and separate loops included), doors and windows in the walls that hold them, columns, rooms with their numbers and names, and roofs (by footprint, those that rise coming in level, and ones by extrusion whose profile is straight lines in a plane square to an axis and whose box the profile and the type's thickness reproduce to a millimetre), converted from feet to millimetres and checked by `Model::check`. Only what a record says is read, and the reply says what is not. Where the record's own box gives a stand-in (a curtain wall as the plane of its box, a sloped or stepped floor, ceiling or roof level at the bottom of its box, a sketch that closes nothing as the footprint of its box, a column as the rectangle of its box) the element comes in as that stand-in and a note in `skipped` says what was not read of it; that is an approximation, and it is not counted as read whole. Anything else the reader cannot decode (a roof by extrusion that is not a straight-line profile, a skylight, a room no walls enclose, stairs, groups, families) is left out and listed in the reply's `skipped` as `N kinds left out, why`. In the desktop, File > Open, the system's open event (Finder, Open With) and a file named on the command line take a `.rvt`: the window stays alive while a box says "Opening a Revit file", asks about unsaved changes first as for any file, and the project that comes in is new and unsaved (Save asks for a `.bimcraft` name; nothing is written back to the `.rvt`, and it is not in File > Open Recent). The status box says how many elements came in and how many were left out, and File > Revit import report lists what came in by category and the notes of what was left out, grouped by cause with their ids. A build without the reader has no `.rvt` option and says why. Joins are BIMCraft's own, and a door's swing is not read. Checked against rvt-rs's own IFC export of the same files, the imported walls, floors, ceilings, openings, columns and roofs agree to a fraction of a millimetre (walls differ where a join is a butt there and a mitre here). A file is read under limits (its size, its streams, what each inflates to) and a damaged or hostile one is an error that says what is wrong. Nothing is taken from inside the file (families, templates, icons) for BIMCraft's own content. Builds that include the reader are Apache-2.0 (see License); `--no-default-features` leaves it out |
| Element ids | Every element, model or annotation, view, sheet or schedule, has an id, six digits from 100000 up, which commands, schedules and the desktop show and take, and a GUID, made once and never changed, as Revit's ElementId and UniqueId: what points at an element (a wall its level, a door its wall, a dimension what it measures, a viewport its view) holds its GUID, so an element that comes in from another file under a new id (Insert from File, `insert`; the same file inserted into itself is copied whole, each copy with a GUID of its own) breaks nothing. IFC writes each element's GUID as its GlobalId and reads it back as one; a file from before GUIDs opens with them, its ids moved up to six digits (1 is 100000). The library has them too: each type, material, picture, family, project parameter, view filter and template, phase, phase filter, design option set and design option has an id (counting down from 999999, so a new project's elements still start at 100000) and a GUID, kept through renames; in a file, whatever names one (a wall's type, a layer's material, a view's template, the phase an element is made in, its values of project parameters, keyed by the parameter's) holds its GUID, so renaming changes nothing in a file but the name. Commands take a library entry by its name or its GUID; `library` lists them, and Insert from File matches them by GUID, then by name. So do their parts: each type's layers and each family's forms and plan symbols hold an id and a GUID, kept while they stay where they are in their list (a type's layers given again, the Family Editor's forms moved), a copy getting its own; a family's types and parameters are library entries, so a component's type and its instance values (keyed by the parameter) are GUIDs in a file, and the materials a family's forms and parameters name too. Inside a family, its forms and types name its own parameters as its formulas do |
| Files | `.bimcraft` projects (JSON, file format 12: every save is 12, so an earlier build refuses even a plain project saved by this one, saying it is from a newer BIMCraft); IFC4 export with storeys, walls swept up from their plan outline (mitred where they join, an arc in short chords) or, attached to a roof, as closed shells, walls, floors, roofs and ceilings with their material layer sets (each material with its colour), slabs (sloped ones as closed shells), ceilings as coverings, spaces and columns, walls, slabs, doors and windows with their `Qto_*BaseQuantities` (a wall's side area and volume gross and less its openings, a slab's area and volume less its openings), beams (`IfcBeam`), footings (`IfcFooting`), pipes (`IfcPipeSegment`), conduits, cable trays and wires (`IfcCableCarrierSegment`, `IfcCableSegment`) and structural columns and floors, each along its own axis and, if structural, with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, the runs of a system assigned to an `IfcSystem` of its name, stairs and ramps as their flights, landings and railings (each railing with its rail's top line as its axis), roofs as closed shells of flat faces (hip, gable, shed or flat), openings that cut the walls and hold the doors and windows, an opening for each slab, ceiling and roof a shaft passes through, masses as building element proxies of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set), and components as furniture, sanitary or waste terminals, pipe fittings, valves, distribution boards, outlets, switching devices, communications appliances, light fixtures or proxies, named `Family:Type` as Revit names them, each form a closed face set in its material's colour, each element's values of the project parameters in a `Project Parameters` property set (dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations belong to views, and stay out of it), and each element's phase and design option in a `BIMCraft_Phasing` property set: its `Phase Created` is always named in it, the first phase too (said to be implied, for another tool to read; a door or window says only what it holds, as one with no phase follows its wall), `Phase Demolished` and `Design Option` where it holds them, and the project's phases in order, with the phase filters, overrides and option sets it changed, in one on the project, and, as IFC says it, its `Status` in its `Pset_*Common` (`EXISTING`, `DEMOLISH`, `NEW` or `TEMPORARY`, for another tool to filter the work by); a project that uses none of it writes none |
| Agents | MCP server, scripts, and every command callable with JSON |

## Quick start

The engine and the CLI need Rust 1.90 or later; the desktop app needs 1.95 (egui 0.36).

```sh
git clone https://github.com/IPedrax/bimcraft
cd bimcraft
cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample       # opens the sample house
```

Without a window:

```sh
cargo build --release
./target/release/bimcraft-cli run --sample --save house.bimcraft --save house.ifc --save plan.png
```

Beside each end is the wall's angle: click it and type a new one, and the wall turns about that end (a wall joined at its other end stays joined, the corner sliding along the wall it meets) | 393 | Edit types | Edit Type opens Type Properties, one dialog for every kind of type, as Revit's: the family and the type at the top with Duplicate and Rename, the type's parameters in a table under group bars that fold (Construction, Dimensions, Materials and Finishes, Graphics, Text…), and OK, Cancel and Apply. Change the type everywhere it's used, Duplicate it into a new one, or Rename it (what's of it follows). A wall type's layers, from the exterior in, or a floor's, roof's or ceiling's, from the top down: each one's function, material and thickness; Insert Layer, and Out and In (Up and Down) and Delete on each | 394 | Place components | Component (CM): pick a family's type in the Type Selector, or in the Project Browser's Families, then click where it goes; Space turns it a quarter turn first. Selected, its own parameters are in Properties, its type's in Type Properties (Edit Type), with Duplicate. Load Family, on Modify \| Place Component, loads a family saved as .json. A door's or a window's family is picked in the Type Selector of the Door or Window tool, or of a selected door or window, as `Family: Type` beside the project's own types, which a new door takes from the project's single door or fixed window; its Edit Type is the family type's | 395 | Family Editor | Manage > New Family (a category's template) and Edit Family (the family of what's selected, or of the component being placed): the family's name and category; Parameters (name, kind, instance, value, formula); Types (a name and the type parameters' values, a blank one the family's own; add, duplicate, delete); Forms (a profile's corners, a circle, a revolve's axis and degrees, a void, its plane, from and to, material and the parameter or formula it's visible by; moved up and down, deleted; Add Box, Cylinder, Revolve, Void); Symbols for a door or window. A preview of the type picked, turned by dragging. Apply makes the project's family what's typed, one undo step; OK also closes; Save Family writes a `.json` file; Load Family reads one; Add to Favorites keeps it in your Favorites | 396 | Favorites | Manage > Favorites: the materials and families you keep for every project, listed with a swatch; Add to Project (under another name when the project has that one) and Remove. A material comes in with the picture its texture is made of, a family with the materials it's made of | 397 | Paint | Modify > Paint (PT), in the 3D view: pick the material in the Options Bar, then click a face; Remove Paint takes it off the face clicked | 398 | Materials | Manage > Materials: the project's library. Pick a material, or New for another, and set its name, colour, cut pattern and surface pattern; Delete takes one out that no layer uses. A layer picks its material from the library. Texture picks a pattern drawn in code, or Picture… a PNG or JPEG file from your disk, for the 3D view; its tile's width and height, angle and offset follow; Save to Favorites keeps the material, and Favorites… opens them | 399 | Project parameters | Manage > Project Parameters: New makes one; name it, choose its type of parameter (text, number, length or yes/no) and the categories it's for. Select an element and its values are under Project Parameters in Properties; empty a field to take a value away | 400 | Schedules | View > Schedules > Schedule/Quantities: pick a category and name it. In Properties, a schedule's Fields, Filter and Sorting/Grouping each open Schedule Properties: add its category's fields, take them away and order them, give one a heading or Calculate totals, add a Calculated Value (`Area * 120`); filter its rows; sort them, and untick Itemize every instance for a row per group. The Room, Door, Window, Wall, Floor and Level Schedules open from the browser, and become the project's once changed. A schedule highlights the rows of what's selected; click a row to select what it lists (Ctrl adds, Shift takes away) | 401 | Views | The Project Browser opens floor plans, ceiling plans, elevations, sections, the 3D view and schedules in tabs; View > Close Inactive closes the others. Its tabs keep it to Views, Schedules, Sheets or Families (Legends are still to come), and its search narrows it as you type, marking what matched: each word must match an entry or a group it's in (`ceiling 2`), `*` stands for any run of characters and `?` for any one. View > Duplicate View (DP) makes a plan view of the plan on screen, plain, with detailing or as a dependent; so does a right click on a plan in the Project Browser, where a plan view also has Delete, and a plan view's name, view range and crop are in Properties as a level's are. The Project Browser's Families lists each system category's types (walls, floors, doors…) and the project's component families; a right click on a type or a family has Delete, which the project refuses while something uses it. Manage > Link Model (LK) links another project, and the Project Browser lists the linked models. Manage > Purge Unused (PU) lists what nothing uses, by kind (types and families checked, as Revit's), and takes it out in one undo step. A right click in any view opens a menu of what it and the selection can do: Cancel, Edit Type, Select All Instances, Delete, Hide Element, Hide Category, Override Graphics, Zoom to Fit, Zoom In, Zoom Out, and in 3D Home View | 402 | Lay out sheets | View > Sheet makes one (A101, A102…); on it, Place View puts a view that's on no sheet yet: a plan, a section or an elevation at its own scale (1 : 100 with none), the 3D view as it's turned on screen, or a schedule. Drag a view or a note to move it, set its scale in Properties, double-click it to open it. File > Export > Sheets as PDF prints them all | 403 | Cut a section, add an elevation | View > Section (CR): click its start and end; it looks to the left of the line, so drawn west to east it looks north. View > Elevation: click beside the building, and it looks at that side. Open them from the browser, or double-click their marks in a plan; in them, click to select what they cut or see | 404 | Look in 3D | The cube on the Quick Access Toolbar (or View > 3D View, or {3D} in the browser) opens the 3D view. Shift and the middle button orbit, as in Revit; the middle button pans, the wheel zooms; Home in the navigation bar goes back to the south-east view. Click to select, or drag a box, as in plan | 405 | Move around | The wheel zooms at the cursor, the middle button pans, the navigation bar or ZF (ZE, ZA) zooms to fit; TL toggles Thin Lines | 406 | Shortcuts | Type a tool's two letters over a view, as in Revit (WA, DR, CR…). CS (Create Similar) starts the tool of the one element selected, with its type picked; SA selects every element of the selected ones' types that the view shows; PP shows or hides Properties; UN opens Project Units; VV (VG) opens Visibility/Graphics, FT Filters and VT View Templates; EH, VH and EU hide an element, a category, or list what's hidden (with Reveal Hidden Elements on, picking a hidden element brings an Unhide Element button, EU too, and VU or Unhide Category its category back); HH, HC, HI, IC, HR and RH hide, isolate, reset and reveal for now; WF, HL and SD set the 3D view's visual style, and GD opens its Graphic Display Options; PH opens Phasing, DO Design Options and DW picks the Demolish tool. KS lists them all, adds your own, changes one, loads a file of them (JSON, Revit's `` lines or `KEY - Name` lines) and restores the defaults; yours are kept in `settings.json`, so they are there the next time BIMCraft starts | 407 | Change theme | View > Dark Mode: choose light, dark, system, or a dark UI with a light canvas; sheets stay white paper | 408 | Arrange the palettes | Drag Properties or the Project Browser by its title: strips along the edges of the view show where it lands, docked down the left or right side or along the bottom (one over another there, or side by side along the bottom), onto another palette's title as a tab of it, or anywhere else to float in a window of its own, which its title moves. Its Dock menu (beside its close button) does the same by name; closed, View > User Interface or PP brings it back where it was | 409 | Float a view | Drag a view's tab off the tab bar, or right-click it and Float: it opens in a window of its own, the active view, and the tools work in it. The views behind stay drawn; a click on one makes it the active view. Drag the window's title back onto the tab bar, or press its Dock button, to make it a tab again. The last tab can't float | 410 | More room | Double-click a ribbon tab (or press the arrow at the right of the tabs) and the ribbon folds to its tabs; a click on a tab then shows its tools over the view until one is picked. Double-click again to open it | 411 | Settings | File > Settings (Ctrl+, or the cog on the Quick Access Toolbar): the theme, language, ribbon and palettes under User Interface, with Plans' two working aids, the origin marker (a small mark at the project's 0, 0 with the directions of x and y) and the view's name in a plan's bottom left corner, both on at first and drawn on the screen only, never in a PNG, a sheet or a printout; background autosave and its interval under Files; whether to look for updates. Performance holds Draw the 3D view on the graphics card (off until you turn it on); the rest of Performance, and Graphics, show settings still to come, greyed out. They're kept in `settings.json` beside the favorites, with where the palettes are | 412 | Units | Manage > Project Units (UN): millimetres, centimetres, metres, inches, feet, or feet and inches. Dimensions, spot elevations, room areas, schedules, Properties and the Options Bar follow; fields read what's typed in those units, or in the unit typed with it, and so do lengths typed while drawing | 413 | Language | View > User Interface > Language: English, Português (Brasil), Español, Čeština, Français, Deutsch, Nederlands or Italiano (and Tiếng Việt, 简体中文 or 繁體中文); the window starts in the system's language (on Windows and macOS, its display language). Manage > Project Language: English, Português (Brasil), Español, Svenska, Čeština, Français, Deutsch, Nederlands or Italiano for what the project's drawings print, and how new levels, views, sheets and rooms are named. A new project takes the window's language when it is also a project language | 414 | Select by ID, IDs of Selection | Manage > Inquiry, as Revit's, and more. Select by ID takes as many IDs, GUIDs or IFC GlobalIds as you paste (from a schedule, a clash report, an IFC viewer), says as you type what it finds and what nothing has, adds to the selection or replaces it, and opens the plan they are in, zoomed to them. IDs of Selection lists each selected element's category, name, ID, GUID and IFC GlobalId, each selectable, and copies one row, a column (IDs, GUIDs, GlobalIds) or all of it, tab-separated for a spreadsheet | 415 | Undo, redo | Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y, or the Quick Access Toolbar. The arrow beside Undo (and Redo) lists the steps, the latest first, named for what each made or took away (Create Walls, Delete Door) or else its command (Move); hovering one marks it and those above it, and a click undoes (or redoes) them all, up to the last 200 | 416 | Start page | Started with no file, the window opens on a start page: New Project and Open, the last ten files as tiles with a picture of each project's 3D view (drawn on a thread of its own; right-click to take one off the list), and along the bottom the source code's page, the version and whether an update is out (with Update now or Download). The quick access bar's Home or Ctrl+D (as in Revit) brings it back over the open project, and Back (top left), Back to the project, Home or Ctrl+D again go back to it as it was | 417 | Files | Ctrl+N, Ctrl+O, Ctrl+S; Open takes IFC files too, and a note says what came in and what was left out; the File tab saves, and exports IFC, the sheets as PDF, and the view on screen as PNG (or a plan as SVG) | 418 | Updates | File > Check for Updates Now looks by hand, and File > Check for updates at startup (on) says whether BIMCraft looks when it starts. A banner under the Options Bar offers a newer version: Update now (for the Windows installer's copy, an AppImage or the macOS app: it downloads and checks the update, then Restart and install asks to save, closes BIMCraft, replaces it and opens the same project again), or Download (every other copy: it opens the release's page), Later (it asks again next time), and Skip this version (not until a newer one) | 419
