## What the reader does with what it cannot read

Where the file says less than BIMCraft's element needs, the reader may take the nearest thing the file does say and put the element
in the project, and the report says what was not read of it. That is an approximation, not a finding about the format, none of
these fallbacks is checked against another reader, and none of them counts as read whole. What the project cannot hold at all is
left out and counted: `N kinds left out, why`, which the desktop adds up.

Measured on the local copies of Autodesk's samples (the files are never committed; `BIMCRAFT_RVT_SAMPLES` names them):

| Sample | Elements in | Left out |
|---|---|---|
| `racbasicsampleproject.rvt` (2023, 2024, 2025) | 118 | 6: 4 rooms the walls do not enclose, 2 skylights |
| `Snowdon Towers Sample Structural.rvt` (2024) | 178 | 0 |
| `Snowdon Towers Sample Architectural.rvt` (2024) | 1,791 | 84: 46 doors and windows that overlap a neighbour in their wall, 36 rooms the walls do not enclose, 2 levels inside other elements |

Stand-ins, each told in the report with its ids:

- A type with no compound structure (a curtain wall, a storefront, a tilted solar panel, a roof type of the 2026 sample) has no
  thickness: a wall takes the thickness its own box gives, and a floor, a ceiling or a roof the height of its box. The panels and
  mullions of a curtain wall, and the layers of such a type, are not read.
- A floor, a ceiling or a roof whose box is taller than its type is thick is sloped or stepped: it comes in level, as thick as its
  type, at the bottom of its box. The slope blocks of the edges (rvt-rs RE-56) are not read, and no sample's slopes were compared
  with another reader's. A wall is never attached to such a roof, because the stand-in is not the roof its top would follow.
- A sketch whose lines do not close joins its open ends by a straight line; one whose loops cross, or one of whose lines has no
  curve, comes in as the footprint of its box. Such a floor's area is not the floor's, and the tests do not compare it.
- A wall whose record holds no curve (a family instance of the wall category, a trellis member) comes in along the long side of
  its own box; one that names no type of the category comes in with a type of its own, as thick as its box says. A turned column
  whose family symbol's size is not known comes in as its box, turned.
- A roof of the class that is neither a roof by footprint nor one by extrusion (a roof by face, over a mass) comes in as the
  footprint of its own box.
- An opening whose box overruns its wall - Revit's frame runs a few millimetres past the wall's box, a door through a wall the file
  cuts short - comes in as far as the wall goes. A sill within 2 mm below the wall's base is taken as zero.

Left out and counted: a window set in a roof or a floor (a skylight; BIMCraft's windows stand in walls), a room no walls enclose
(Revit's own not-enclosed room, or one bounded by room separation lines, which BIMCraft has none of: it comes in again when the
walls enclose its box), a level inside another element (a group's, a family's), and an opening the model's rules refuse where it
overlaps a neighbour in its wall. The last is the rule `Model::check` applies to every project: it counts two openings as
overlapping where they share a place along the wall, whatever their heights, so a window over a door is refused. Letting openings
overlap only where they also share a height would bring the 46 of the Snowdon sample in; that is a change of the model's rule,
for every project, and is made on its own.

  later, with their levels, walls, floors and columns (`autodesks_2018_samples_come_in_through_the_readers_made_for_2023`); they
  were not compared with rvt-rs. A workshared file is covered by no Autodesk sample. One workshared Revit 2018 file the project owner gave (a pipework and ductwork project: 9 levels, 68,811 element records) reads with the rows above: its levels, walls, floor, 4,407 of 4,410 pipes, 1,194 ducts and 31 cable trays come in as what they are, 8,847 fittings, fixtures, equipment and terminals as boxes, and 3,348 elements of categories the name table above has not as boxes of a family named by the category's id (nothing here says what they are, so they are not guessed at). What is left out is listed in the notes: 23,554 model lines, which have no reader, 11,664 companions of the pipes, fittings, ducts, duct fittings and flex ducts whose box is that element's (the last finding above), and 2,242 elements whose box has no volume. - The element readers have not been compared with rvt-rs on anything but the basic samples; Snowdon Towers (1,062 walls) was

- A roof by extrusion with an arc (a barrel vault), one in a plane at an angle, or one that rises in steps: the one real roof is a gable, and

  Snowdon Towers: storefront, glazing and solar-panel types and one type named `_Not Defined`) holds a width the reader can find (the data of the eight Snowdon types that have any is 350 to 402 bytes, and the only lengths in it are a
  curtain grid's spacings; the architectural sample's type has no data object at all), so none comes in as a single layer; each is left out and listed under its type's name. The categories `info` prints as bare ids: no table of Autodesk's

- What no sample sets: a roof slope (rvt-rs's RE-56 is not ported), a curved wall that hosts an opening (left out; one at an angle is solved from the box, checked on the Snowdon sample only), a
  door's swing and hand, a column's section shape (round, L, I, tube: the box is imported), a sloped or stepped floor (left out),
  curtain walls and their doors (left out), groups, stairs, railings, and a wall's join list (RE-127).
- The desktop's File > Open reads a file on a thread of its own and shows the import report; it has been driven by tests with a stand-in
  reader and by hand on the samples, not on a Mac or Windows.

## What the reader does with what it cannot read

Where the file says less than BIMCraft's element needs, the reader may take the nearest thing the file does say and put the element
in the project, and the report says what was not read of it. That is an approximation, not a finding about the format, none of
these fallbacks is checked against another reader, and none of them counts as read whole. What the project cannot hold at all is
left out and counted: `N kinds left out, why`, which the desktop adds up.

Measured on the local copies of Autodesk's samples (the files are never committed; `BIMCRAFT_RVT_SAMPLES` names them):

| Sample | Elements in | Left out |
|---|---|---|
| `racbasicsampleproject.rvt` (2023, 2024, 2025) | 118 | 6: 4 rooms the walls do not enclose, 2 skylights |
| `Snowdon Towers Sample Structural.rvt` (2024) | 178 | 0 |
| `Snowdon Towers Sample Architectural.rvt` (2024) | 1,791 | 84: 46 doors and windows that overlap a neighbour in their wall, 36 rooms the walls do not enclose, 2 levels inside other elements |

Stand-ins, each told in the report with its ids:

- A type with no compound structure (a curtain wall, a storefront, a tilted solar panel, a roof type of the 2026 sample) has no
  thickness: a wall takes the thickness its own box gives, and a floor, a ceiling or a roof the height of its box. The panels and
  mullions of a curtain wall, and the layers of such a type, are not read.
- A floor, a ceiling or a roof whose box is taller than its type is thick is sloped or stepped: it comes in level, as thick as its
  type, at the bottom of its box. The slope blocks of the edges (rvt-rs RE-56) are not read, and no sample's slopes were compared
  with another reader's. A wall is never attached to such a roof, because the stand-in is not the roof its top would follow.
- A sketch whose lines do not close joins its open ends by a straight line; one whose loops cross, or one of whose lines has no
  curve, comes in as the footprint of its box. Such a floor's area is not the floor's, and the tests do not compare it.
- A wall whose record holds no curve (a family instance of the wall category, a trellis member) comes in along the long side of
  its own box; one that names no type of the category comes in with a type of its own, as thick as its box says. A turned column
  whose family symbol's size is not known comes in as its box, turned.
- A roof of the class that is neither a roof by footprint nor one by extrusion (a roof by face, over a mass) comes in as the
  footprint of its own box.
- An opening whose box overruns its wall - Revit's frame runs a few millimetres past the wall's box, a door through a wall the file
  cuts short - comes in as far as the wall goes. A sill within 2 mm below the wall's base is taken as zero.

Left out and counted: a window set in a roof or a floor (a skylight; BIMCraft's windows stand in walls), a room no walls enclose
(Revit's own not-enclosed room, or one bounded by room separation lines, which BIMCraft has none of: it comes in again when the
walls enclose its box), a level inside another element (a group's, a family's), and an opening the model's rules refuse where it
overlaps a neighbour in its wall. The last is the rule `Model::check` applies to every project: it counts two openings as
overlapping where they share a place along the wall, whatever their heights, so a window over a door is refused. Letting openings
overlap only where they also share a height would bring the 46 of the Snowdon sample in; that is a change of the model's rule,
for every project, and is made on its own.

One workshared Revit 2018 file the project owner gave (a pipework and ductwork project: 9 levels, 68,811 element records) reads with the rows above: its levels, walls, floor, 4,407 of 4,410 pipes, 1,194 ducts and 31 cable trays come in as what they are, 8,847 fittings, fixtures, equipment and terminals as boxes, and 3,348 elements of categories the name table above has not as boxes of a family named by the category's id (nothing here says what they are, so they are not guessed at). A pipe, duct or tray is not connected to its neighbours, and a fitting is a box, not an elbow or a tee.
- The element readers have not been compared with rvt-rs on anything but the basic samples; Snowdon Towers (1,062 walls) was

# Point clouds

On the roadmap under 0.9 Interoperability. A project holds scans and places them, the 3D view, plans and sections draw them,
plans snap to them, and the desktop brings them in (Insert > Point Cloud). IFC leaves them out, as Revit's export does: IFC4 has
no point cloud, and `ifc_leaves_scans_out_as_revit_does` keeps the file what it was without them.

Point clouds (`cloud.rs`) come from public specifications: PTS and XYZ text, PLY (text or either byte order) and ASPRS LAS 1.0
to 1.4 uncompressed, and ASTM E57 (`Format::from_extension` says why LAZ and ReCap's RCP/RCS don't). `cloud::read` parses a file twice,
once to measure it (`Stats`: the count, the bounds, the ranges of intensity and colour) and once to keep it: every `stride`th
point so `Options::cap` is never passed, then one in each cube of `spacing`, the same every time. A `Scan` keeps its points as
`f32` about `origin`, the middle of its bounds, so a survey's coordinates far off keep their millimetres within `MAX_SPAN`;
colour comes in eight bits whether the file has eight, sixteen or nought to one, and intensity alone is grey.

E57 (ASTM E2807, `cloud/e57.rs`) is read from the standard with no library: the 48-byte header, pages of 1024 bytes whose last
four are a CRC-32C (`Paged` reads the 1020 logical bytes of each; the checksums aren't checked, so a page that lies reads as
points that lie, never a crash), and the XML section, read by a small parser of its own (elements, attributes, text, CDATA;
capped in depth and size). Every `data3D` scan comes in, placed by its `pose` (a quaternion and a translation), as one `Scan`
whose `read` is the sum of their `recordCount`s. Each scan's points are a CompressedVector: a section header, then data packets
whose bytestreams, one for each field of the `prototype`, are bit-packed and run on from packet to packet; `Pack` decodes
Float (single or double), Integer and ScaledInteger, and only bit-packing, the one codec E57 writes, is read. Cartesian or
spherical coordinates both come in, a point marked invalid doesn't, and colour is scaled from `colorLimits` (or its field's
range) to eight bits. `images2D` is passed over. A file is held to `Caps` before anything is unpacked: up to 4096 scans, 100 million
points in all of them, 32 fields to a point, no two scans on one section, a section with room for the bits its count asks for (a
field of no bits is legal, so eight points can share a byte), and no stream more than 4 MiB ahead of the others. The tests write E57 files of their own (`e57` in the module's tests), with
values that cross packets and pages; the reference survey's 177 MB file reads its 6.6 million points in under two seconds.

A project holds each scan once, by name, as a `Cloud` in `Model::clouds` (a library entry of kind `Cloud`, so it has an id and a
GUID): its points and colours shared behind an `Arc`, the file it came from, and where its middle was there. A project file holds
it as `CloudFile`, the points as little-endian `f32` and the colours as bytes, each deflated and in base64, packed once and kept
(`Cloud::file`); coming back, every check `Cloud::new` makes is made again, and what unpacks past `MAX_CLOUD_POINTS` stops there.
A project holds up to `MAX_CLOUDS` scans and `MAX_CLOUD_POINTS` points among them (`Model::check`), so the `point_cloud` command
thins a new one to what the others leave. A project file is held to the same while it is read, not after: `Model::clouds` reads
through `cloud::deserialize_scans`, which refuses the entry past the count, and the scan that takes the points past the budget,
before unpacking the next (unpacking is where the memory goes, and the file is read twice, by the lenient walk and the strict read).

A survey's stations come in as one scan, as ReCap gathers a project's scans and Revit links the project: `path` may be a list of
up to `MAX_STATIONS` files. Each is read with an even share of what the project leaves, and `cloud::merge` puts them about the
middle of them all, keeps one point in each cube of `spacing` across them (so where stations overlap they aren't kept twice), and
greys a file with no colours among ones with. The `Cloud` keeps a `Station` for each file, its name and its share of the points
in order, so a view may one day show or hide a station; it is known by the first file's name, and the element's JSON lists the
stations. A list of one is that file alone.

A `PointCloud` element places a scan, as a component places a family: its `cloud` (a library name, a GUID in a file), its `level`,
its middle at `at` and `offset` over the level, turned `angle` degrees about it; `Model::cloud_place` is that transform and
`Model::cloud_box` the box round what it places. It holds no `params`, so phases, design options and paint don't reach it. It moves,
turns and copies as any element; it doesn't mirror, since a scan is what was measured. The `point_cloud` command brings a file in
(`path`) or places a held scan again (`cloud`); by default its middle goes on `at` and its foot on the level (Revit's Auto - Center
to Center), and with `origin: file` where the file's coordinates put it (Origin to Origin) when that is within `MAX_COORD`. A scan
that nothing places any more goes after the command that left it so (`Model::unplaced_clouds`, in `Session::execute`), and undo
brings it back with its element. Insert from File brings the scan with the element. IFC export leaves scans out.

The 3D view (`view3d.rs`) keeps each placed scan as a `Scan`: its points and colours shared with the model's, and where they
go. After the opaque surfaces are rasterised, `Scene::dots` draws each point as a square [`DOT`] pixels wide into the same
depth buffer, so what is nearer hides a scan and a scan hides what is behind it, and what the view sees through is drawn over
it. A point's pixel holds its scan's slot after the triangles', so it picks, box-selects and tints as its element; it has no
face to paint and draws no edge. Points are not lit: they keep the scan's colours, grey (`cloud::GREY`) for a scan with none,
or the colour the view's projection fill gives. A picture draws at most `DRAWN` points, an even share of each scan's past
that, as Revit's density does. The view fits round its scans, and a level's plane reaches past them (`Model::model_extent`).
A 3D view's section box keeps a scan's points inside it and no others, so its floors and ceilings can be cut away to show the walls to
model against ([views and graphics](views-and-graphics.md)); in a plan the view range does it, or the box itself when the plan follows it. Views hide and override point clouds by element or by the category `pointcloud` (`graphics::SCANS`, apart from `MODEL`:
Revit has a tab of its own for them in Visibility/Graphics, and Object Styles no row). The graphics card doesn't draw them
yet: `gpu::Mesh::new` refuses a view that shows one, and the processor draws it. The wireframe style leaves them out.

A section's or an elevation's picture is the same rasteriser with a `Clip`, and `Scene::dots` keeps a point as `raster` keeps a
pixel: between the line and the far clip, inside the crop. A plan draws what its view range sees, from the cut plane down to
the view depth (`render::scans`, under everything else), from above: each point a dot `DOT` pixels wide in its colour or the
view's, the highest at each pixel on top, `DRAWN` among the scans as in 3D. Each scan is one `Prim::Image` owned by its
element, no bigger than its dots and clear between them; a picture picks where it isn't clear (`drawn_near` in `Drawing::pick_all`),
so a click between a scan's points finds what is there, and a sheet's opaque pictures pick as they did. A PDF masks a picture
that isn't all there with its alpha (`/SMask`), and an SVG holds it as a PNG. A reflected ceiling plan leaves scans out. The
desktop's plan canvas loads a drawing's pictures as textures once for as long as it is shown (`PlanCache::pictures`) and, on a
dark canvas, dims them so the lightened ink over them still reads. A scan the view fills with one colour (its projection's fill,
`Look::filled`) is ink itself: its picture is marked `ink` and the dark canvas leaves it undimmed.

A scan's own colours are mid-tones that read poorly over paper or the dark canvas, so the view control bar (`footer.rs`) has
High Contrast Point Clouds wherever the project or a model it links holds a scan (the bar asks the model the views draw whether it holds
one, which is cheap because a command drops a scan nothing places): it fills the view's `pointcloud` category with `HIGH_CONTRAST`, a
crimson that reads on both and apart from the model's black lines (or the colour the user picks in Settings > Graphics, kept
as `high_contrast` in `settings.json` and read back only when it is `[r, g, b]`), through the `graphics` command (merged into the category's
override, so its halftone or lines stay), and again takes the fill away. It is lit whenever the category has a fill, whoever set
it, and greyed out when a view template controls the categories. It sets the category's override and no other: `Look::of` applies the
category's, then each view filter's, then the element's own, the last prevailing, so a scan given a colour of its own in
Visibility/Graphics (or picked out by a filter that fills) keeps it whatever the button does. The button is lit for the category
and can't tell, since what the scans come to is the whole `Look` for every frame of the bar; its tooltip says so instead.

A plan snaps to a scan where its cut plane cuts it, to trace what was measured: of the points within `snap::CUT_BAND` of the cut,
the nearest to the cursor seen from above (`Kind::Point`, "Point Cloud", switched by `Snaps::cloud` in Manage > Snaps). It comes
after what the model has to snap to (ends, middles, centres, crossings), so a wall's end beats a point nearer the cursor, and
before the perpendicular, the angle guides and a wall's centre line. `snap::cloud_point` turns the cursor into each shown scan's
own terms and asks `Cloud::nearest`, which looks only in the squares of the scan's `Grid` (its points by `CELL` mm squares from
above, made the first time something snaps to it and shared by its clones) that the reach touches, so a snap on millions of points
costs microseconds.

In the desktop (`clouds.rs`), Insert > Point Cloud, in the Insert tab's Link panel beside Link Model as in Revit, asks for one
file or several (`BimApp::ask_files`: a dialog's answer is a list of paths now) and opens `CloudBox`: its name (the first file's),
the units of its coordinates, a spacing, and Revit's positioning, Auto - Center to Center or Auto - Origin to Origin. OK runs
`point_cloud` on the level of the plan on screen and selects what it placed; a refusal stays in the box with its reason
(`point_cloud_paths` opens the box, what a test hands the files to). The Properties palette shows a point cloud's level and offset
(edited), its scan, file and points, its origin and angle; Visibility/Graphics lists `pointcloud` after the model's categories.
# Importing and linking CAD drawings

On the roadmap under 0.9 Interoperability, as Revit's Import CAD and Link CAD: a consultant's or a surveyor's DXF drawing
brought into a project and drawn under the model in the plans of a level, to trace walls over and to check against. A project
holds each drawing once, an import element places it, plans draw and snap to it, and the desktop brings one in (Insert > Import
CAD, Link CAD). A DWG comes in as the DXF it becomes (below); DXF export, exploding an import into detail lines (which waits on detail lines, issue #58), and
images and PDFs as underlays are still to come.

## The reader

`dxf.rs` reads ASCII DXF of any version from Autodesk's public DXF reference: pairs of a group code and a value, read in
sections. From the header it takes `$INSUNITS` (the drawing's unit, `Dxf::unit` and `Dxf::scale`, mm to each of its units),
`$ACADVER` and `$LTSCALE`; from the tables its layers (colour, off when the colour is negative, frozen by flag, linetype, line
weight) and its linetypes' dash patterns; from the blocks section the blocks; and from the entities section what model space
draws (an entity with code 67 set is paper space's, and left out). Entities come in as a short list of `Shape`s, in the
drawing's own units: LINE, LWPOLYLINE and POLYLINE (bulges become arcs; a 3D mesh or polyface is left out), CIRCLE, ARC,
ELLIPSE (as a polyline), SPLINE (its fit points, else its control points), POINT, TEXT and MTEXT (its formatting codes taken

# Point clouds

On the roadmap under 0.9 Interoperability. A project holds scans and places them, the 3D view, plans and sections draw them,
plans snap to them, and the desktop brings them in (Insert > Point Cloud). IFC leaves them out, as Revit's export does: IFC4 has
no point cloud, and `ifc_leaves_scans_out_as_revit_does` keeps the file what it was without them.

Point clouds (`cloud.rs`) come from public specifications: PTS and XYZ text, PLY (text or either byte order) and ASPRS LAS 1.0
to 1.4 uncompressed, and ASTM E57 (`Format::from_extension` says why LAZ and ReCap's RCP/RCS don't). `cloud::read` parses a file twice,
once to measure it (`Stats`: the count, the bounds, the ranges of intensity and colour) and once to keep it: every `stride`th
point so `Options::cap` is never passed, then one in each cube of `spacing`, the same every time. A `Scan` keeps its points as
`f32` about `origin`, the middle of its bounds, so a survey's coordinates far off keep their millimetres within `MAX_SPAN`;
colour comes in eight bits whether the file has eight, sixteen or nought to one, and intensity alone is grey.

E57 (ASTM E2807, `cloud/e57.rs`) is read from the standard with no library: the 48-byte header, pages of 1024 bytes whose last
four are a CRC-32C (`Paged` reads the 1020 logical bytes of each; the checksums aren't checked, so a page that lies reads as
points that lie, never a crash), and the XML section, read by a small parser of its own (elements, attributes, text, CDATA;
capped in depth and size). Every `data3D` scan comes in, placed by its `pose` (a quaternion and a translation), as one `Scan`
whose `read` is the sum of their `recordCount`s. Each scan's points are a CompressedVector: a section header, then data packets
whose bytestreams, one for each field of the `prototype`, are bit-packed and run on from packet to packet; `Pack` decodes
Float (single or double), Integer and ScaledInteger, and only bit-packing, the one codec E57 writes, is read. Cartesian or
spherical coordinates both come in, a point marked invalid doesn't, and colour is scaled from `colorLimits` (or its field's
range) to eight bits. `images2D` is passed over. A file is held to `Caps` before anything is unpacked: up to 4096 scans, 100 million
points in all of them, 32 fields to a point, no two scans on one section, a section with room for the bits its count asks for (a
field of no bits is legal, so eight points can share a byte), and no stream more than 4 MiB ahead of the others. The tests write E57 files of their own (`e57` in the module's tests), with
values that cross packets and pages; the reference survey's 177 MB file reads its 6.6 million points in under two seconds.

A project holds each scan once, by name, as a `Cloud` in `Model::clouds` (a library entry of kind `Cloud`, so it has an id and a
GUID): its points and colours shared behind an `Arc`, the file it came from, and where its middle was there. A project file holds
it as `CloudFile`, the points as little-endian `f32` and the colours as bytes, each deflated and in base64, packed once and kept
(`Cloud::file`); coming back, every check `Cloud::new` makes is made again, and what unpacks past `MAX_CLOUD_POINTS` stops there.
A project holds up to `MAX_CLOUDS` scans and `MAX_CLOUD_POINTS` points among them (`Model::check`), so the `point_cloud` command
thins a new one to what the others leave. A project file is held to the same while it is read, not after: `Model::clouds` reads
through `cloud::deserialize_scans`, which refuses the entry past the count, and the scan that takes the points past the budget,
before unpacking the next (unpacking is where the memory goes, and the file is read twice, by the lenient walk and the strict read).

A survey's stations come in as one scan, as ReCap gathers a project's scans and Revit links the project: `path` may be a list of
up to `MAX_STATIONS` files. Each is read with an even share of what the project leaves, and `cloud::merge` puts them about the
middle of them all, keeps one point in each cube of `spacing` across them (so where stations overlap they aren't kept twice), and
greys a file with no colours among ones with. The `Cloud` keeps a `Station` for each file, its name and its share of the points
in order, so a view may one day show or hide a station; it is known by the first file's name, and the element's JSON lists the
stations. A list of one is that file alone.

A `PointCloud` element places a scan, as a component places a family: its `cloud` (a library name, a GUID in a file), its `level`,
its middle at `at` and `offset` over the level, turned `angle` degrees about it; `Model::cloud_place` is that transform and
`Model::cloud_box` the box round what it places. It holds no `params`, so phases, design options and paint don't reach it. It moves,
turns and copies as any element; it doesn't mirror, since a scan is what was measured. The `point_cloud` command brings a file in
(`path`) or places a held scan again (`cloud`); by default its middle goes on `at` and its foot on the level (Revit's Auto - Center
to Center), and with `origin: file` where the file's coordinates put it (Origin to Origin) when that is within `MAX_COORD`. A scan
that nothing places any more goes after the command that left it so (`Model::unplaced_clouds`, in `Session::execute`), and undo
brings it back with its element. Insert from File brings the scan with the element. IFC export leaves scans out.

The 3D view (`view3d.rs`) keeps each placed scan as a `Scan`: its points and colours shared with the model's, and where they
go. After the opaque surfaces are rasterised, `Scene::dots` draws each point as a square [`DOT`] pixels wide into the same
depth buffer, so what is nearer hides a scan and a scan hides what is behind it, and what the view sees through is drawn over
it. A point's pixel holds its scan's slot after the triangles', so it picks, box-selects and tints as its element; it has no
face to paint and draws no edge. Points are not lit: they keep the scan's colours, grey (`cloud::GREY`) for a scan with none,
or the colour the view's projection fill gives. A picture draws at most `DRAWN` points, an even share of each scan's past
that, as Revit's density does. The view fits round its scans, and a level's plane reaches past them (`Model::model_extent`).
A 3D view's section box keeps a scan's points inside it and no others, so its floors and ceilings can be cut away to show the walls to
model against ([views and graphics](views-and-graphics.md)); in a plan the view range does it, or the box itself when the plan follows it. Views hide and override point clouds by element or by the category `pointcloud` (`graphics::SCANS`, apart from `MODEL`:
Revit has a tab of its own for them in Visibility/Graphics, and Object Styles no row). The graphics card doesn't draw them
yet: `gpu::Mesh::new` refuses a view that shows one, and the processor draws it. The wireframe style leaves them out.

A section's or an elevation's picture is the same rasteriser with a `Clip`, and `Scene::dots` keeps a point as `raster` keeps a
pixel: between the line and the far clip, inside the crop. A plan draws what its view range sees, from the cut plane down to
the view depth (`render::scans`, under everything else), from above: each point a dot `DOT` pixels wide in its colour or the
view's, the highest at each pixel on top, `DRAWN` among the scans as in 3D. Each scan is one `Prim::Image` owned by its
element, no bigger than its dots and clear between them; a picture picks where it isn't clear (`drawn_near` in `Drawing::pick_all`),
so a click between a scan's points finds what is there, and a sheet's opaque pictures pick as they did. A PDF masks a picture
that isn't all there with its alpha (`/SMask`), and an SVG holds it as a PNG. A reflected ceiling plan leaves scans out. The
desktop's plan canvas loads a drawing's pictures as textures once for as long as it is shown (`PlanCache::pictures`) and, on a
dark canvas, dims them so the lightened ink over them still reads. A scan the view fills with one colour (its projection's fill,
`Look::filled`) is ink itself: its picture is marked `ink` and the dark canvas leaves it undimmed.

A scan's own colours are mid-tones that read poorly over paper or the dark canvas, so the view control bar (`footer.rs`) has
High Contrast Point Clouds wherever the project or a model it links holds a scan (the bar asks the model the views draw whether it holds
one, which is cheap because a command drops a scan nothing places): it fills the view's `pointcloud` category with `HIGH_CONTRAST`, a
crimson that reads on both and apart from the model's black lines (or the colour the user picks in Settings > Graphics, kept
as `high_contrast` in `settings.json` and read back only when it is `[r, g, b]`), through the `graphics` command (merged into the category's
override, so its halftone or lines stay), and again takes the fill away. It is lit whenever the category has a fill, whoever set
it, and greyed out when a view template controls the categories. It sets the category's override and no other: `Look::of` applies the
category's, then each view filter's, then the element's own, the last prevailing, so a scan given a colour of its own in
Visibility/Graphics (or picked out by a filter that fills) keeps it whatever the button does. The button is lit for the category
and can't tell, since what the scans come to is the whole `Look` for every frame of the bar; its tooltip says so instead.

A plan snaps to a scan where its cut plane cuts it, to trace what was measured: of the points within `snap::CUT_BAND` of the cut,
the nearest to the cursor seen from above (`Kind::Point`, "Point Cloud", switched by `Snaps::cloud` in Manage > Snaps). It comes
after what the model has to snap to (ends, middles, centres, crossings), so a wall's end beats a point nearer the cursor, and
before the perpendicular, the angle guides and a wall's centre line. `snap::cloud_point` turns the cursor into each shown scan's
own terms and asks `Cloud::nearest`, which looks only in the squares of the scan's `Grid` (its points by `CELL` mm squares from
above, made the first time something snaps to it and shared by its clones) that the reach touches, so a snap on millions of points
costs microseconds.

In the desktop (`clouds.rs`), Insert > Point Cloud, in the Insert tab's Link panel beside Link Model as in Revit, asks for one
file or several (`BimApp::ask_files`: a dialog's answer is a list of paths now) and opens `CloudBox`: its name (the first file's),

`point_cloud` on the level of the plan on screen and selects what it placed; a refusal stays in the box with its reason
(`point_cloud_paths` opens the box, what a test hands the files to). The Properties palette shows a point cloud's level and offset
(edited), its scan, file and points, its origin and angle; Visibility/Graphics lists `pointcloud` after the model's categories.

{point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it
## sketch [] | Sketch | None
{lines: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} solves a sketch without making anything, as Finish Edit Mode does: lines in any order, either way round, joined end to end (within 1 mm) into closed loops; a loop inside no other (or inside a hole) an outline, counter-clockwise, one inside an outline a hole in it, clockwise. Gives each region's `outline`, `holes` and `area_m2`, or every problem with the lines it's about (numbered from 0): ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line too: a polyline round a bow tie crosses itself), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight pieces its lines are drawn with (an arc, a circle or a curve is cut into chords, a circle into up to 8,193): past 200,000 of them, or when they lie so close together that telling which cross takes more than six million steps, it is refused at once. `sketch` on floor, ceiling, roof and shaft, and edit_boundary, take the same lines for one outline and its holes
## shaft [] | Shaft Opening | Architecture > Shaft
{boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`
## edit_boundary [] | Edit Boundary | None
{id, sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} redraws a floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's footprint's or a shaft's outline and its holes (a floor's or a ceiling's openings, a roof's courtyards; a shaft has none) as a sketch, all at once (see `sketch`); a roof's gable edges stay gables where the new footprint has the same edge. Without `sketch`, gives the outline and holes it has now, as the lines to edit. The outline must be simple, as `floor` says; a line that crosses itself is found as two that cross are
## edit_shape [] | Modify Sub Elements | None
{id, points?: [{at: [x,y], z, id?}, …], lines?: [{a: [x,y], b: [x,y], id?}, …], absolute?} gives a floor's top, or a flat roof's by footprint (its underside following), its shape anew, all at once: points `z` mm above (negative, below) where its top would be without them (with `absolute`, at that elevation), and split lines it folds along, between which it's flat triangles, merged where neighbours lie in one plane: falls to drains, ridges, valleys. Its outline's and openings' corners stay at 0 unless a point is there; a line's end that is no point and no corner becomes a point at the height the top has there. Sent back with its `id`, a point or a line keeps it. A shaped floor has no slope arrow, a shaped roof no `slope`. Without `points` or `lines`, gives the shape: its points and lines with their ids, its corners at their heights, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest (`top`, mm above zero)
## add_point [] | Add Point | None
{id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height
## add_split_line [] | Add Split Line | None
{id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now
## reset_shape [] | Reset Shape | None
{id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again
## falls [] | Falls | None
{id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest. Refused, saying why and where: a corner a drain can reach only over the outline or a ridge, or a plane that can't fall as asked to a drain
## mass ['MS'] | Mass | None
{boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`
## mass_floors ['MF'] | Mass Floors | None
{mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level
## wall_by_face ['WB'] | Wall by Face | None
{mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on
## floor_by_face ['FB'] | Floor by Face | None
{mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on
## roof_by_face ['RB'] | Roof by Face | None
{mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on
## update_by_face ['UF'] | Update to Face | None
{mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`
## show_mass ['MH'] | Show Mass | None
{view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's
## room ['RM'] | Room | Architecture > Room
{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen
## room_separator [] | Room Separator | None
{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids
## rebar [] | Rebar | None
{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule
## reinforce [] | Reinforce | None
{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes
## reinforcement_preset [] | Reinforcement Presets | None
{name?, kind?: beam|column|footing|floor, params?, rename?, delete?: true} a named set of the parameters `reinforce` takes for one kind of host (`params`: its `cover`, `grade`, `grade_stirrup`, `clearance` and what its kind takes, and not `host`), kept in the project; `reinforce` with `preset` takes it and lets what is given with it replace its own. Without `name`, lists them. It is not checked against any host until it arms one
## voltage [] | Voltage Definitions | None
{name?, nominal?, min?, max?, rename?, delete?: true} a voltage of the project's electrical settings, in volts: `nominal`, and the band a device may read within, `min` to `max` (10 per cent either way unless given). Without `name`, lists them. A voltage a distribution system names cannot be deleted; renamed, the systems follow
## distribution_system [] | Distribution Systems | None
{name?, phases?: 1|2|3, wires?, l_l?, l_n?, l_g?, ground?, rename?, delete?: true} a distribution system of the project's electrical settings. `wires` counts the line conductors and the neutral, not the protective one (3 phases: 3 or 4). `l_l`, `l_n` and `l_g` name the voltages between two lines, a line and the neutral, and a line and earth (at least one; `l_l` from 2 phases; with 3 phases `l_l` is about 1.73 times `l_n`), each a `voltage` of the project; "" takes one away. `ground` is the earthing: TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT or IT. A voltage the project lacks is refused, and the refusal lists the ones it has. Without `name`, lists them
## wire_type [] | Wire Types | None
{name?, material?: copper|aluminium, temperature?, insulation?, note?, sizes?: [{section, ampacity, label?}], rename?, delete?: true} a wire type of the project's electrical settings: a conductor's `material`, working `temperature` (°C) and `insulation`, and its table, `sizes`: the `section` of each row in mm² (smallest first, never less than the row before) and the `ampacity` it carries in amperes, with a `label` for how its standard names it (12 AWG). Giving `sizes` replaces the table. `note` says where the ampacities come from. Without `name`, lists them
## column ['CL'] | Column | Architecture > Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`
## structural_column ['CL'] | Structural Column | None
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one
## footing ['FI'] | Isolated Footing | None
{at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below
## beam ['BM'] | Beam | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°
## strip_footing ['FW'] | Wall Footing | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)
## pipe ['PI'] | Pipe | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")
## duct ['DU'] | Duct | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Supply air", "Exhaust")
## conduit ['CN'] | Conduit | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit
## cable_tray ['CT'] | Cable Tray | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep
## wire ['EW'] | Wire | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit
## down_conductor ['DC'] | Down Conductor | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to
## ground_conductor ['GC'] | Earthing Conductor | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)
## cabling ['CB'] | Cabling | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to
## stair [] | Stair | Architecture > Stair
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). 36	{id, at: [x, y], reach?} what of a CAD import lies nearest `at`, within `reach` mm (100 unless given): its kind, layer, colour, linetype and weight, as Revit's Query
37	## wall ['WA'] | Wall | Architecture > Wall
38	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them
39	## door ['DR'] | Door | Architecture > Door
40	{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door
41	## window ['WN'] | Window | Architecture > Window
42	{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)
43	## floor [] | Floor | Architecture > Floor
44	{boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline
45	## ceiling [] | Ceiling | Architecture > Ceiling
46	{point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it
47	## sketch [] | Sketch | None
48	{lines: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} solves a sketch without making anything, as Finish Edit Mode does: lines in any order, either way round, joined end to end (within 1 mm) into closed loops; a loop inside no other (or inside a hole) an outline, counter-clockwise, one inside an outline a hole in it, clockwise. Gives each region's `outline`, `holes` and `area_m2`, or every problem with the lines it's about (numbered from 0): ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line too: a polyline round a bow tie crosses itself), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight pieces its lines are drawn with (an arc, a circle or a curve is cut into chords, a circle into up to 8,193): past 200,000 of them, or when they lie so close together that telling which cross takes more than six million steps, it is refused at once. `sketch` on floor, ceiling, roof and shaft, and edit_boundary, take the same lines for one outline and its holes
49	## shaft [] | Shaft Opening | Architecture > Shaft
50	{boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`
51	## edit_boundary [] | Edit Boundary | None
52	{id, sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} redraws a floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's footprint's or a shaft's outline and its holes (a floor's or a ceiling's openings, a roof's courtyards; a shaft has none) as a sketch, all at once (see `sketch`); a roof's gable edges stay gables where the new footprint has the same edge. Without `sketch`, gives the outline and holes it has now, as the lines to edit. The outline must be simple, as `floor` says; a line that crosses itself is found as two that cross are
53	## edit_shape [] | Modify Sub Elements | None
54	{id, points?: [{at: [x,y], z, id?}, …], lines?: [{a: [x,y], b: [x,y], id?}, …], absolute?} gives a floor's top, or a flat roof's by footprint (its underside following), its shape anew, all at once: points `z` mm above (negative, below) where its top would be without them (with `absolute`, at that elevation), and split lines it folds along, between which it's flat triangles, merged where neighbours lie in one plane: falls to drains, ridges, valleys. Its outline's and openings' corners stay at 0 unless a point is there; a line's end that is no point and no corner becomes a point at the height the top has there. Sent back with its `id`, a point or a line keeps it. A shaped floor has no slope arrow, a shaped roof no `slope`. Without `points` or `lines`, gives the shape: its points and lines with their ids, its corners at their heights, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest (`top`, mm above zero)
55	## add_point [] | Add Point | None
56	{id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height
57	## add_split_line [] | Add Split Line | None
58	{id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now
59	## reset_shape [] | Reset Shape | None
60	{id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again
61	## falls [] | Falls | None
62	{id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest. Refused, saying why and where: a corner a drain can reach only over the outline or a ridge, or a plane that can't fall as asked to a drain
63	## mass ['MS'] | Mass | None
64	{boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`
65	## mass_floors ['MF'] | Mass Floors | None
66	{mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level
67	## wall_by_face ['WB'] | Wall by Face | None
68	{mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on
69	## floor_by_face ['FB'] | Floor by Face | None
70	{mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on
71	## roof_by_face ['RB'] | Roof by Face | None
72	{mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on
73	## update_by_face ['UF'] | Update to Face | None
74	{mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`
75	## show_mass ['MH'] | Show Mass | None
76	{view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's
77	## room ['RM'] | Room | Architecture > Room
78	{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen
79	## room_separator [] | Room Separator | None
80	{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids
81	## rebar [] | Rebar | None
82	{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule
83	## reinforce [] | Reinforce | None
84	{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes
85	## reinforcement_preset [] | Reinforcement Presets | None
86	{name?, kind?: beam|column|footing|floor, params?, rename?, delete?: true} a named set of the parameters `reinforce` takes for one kind of host (`params`: its `cover`, `grade`, `grade_stirrup`, `clearance` and what its kind takes, and not `host`), kept in the project; `reinforce` with `preset` takes it and lets what is given with it replace its own. Without `name`, lists them. It is not checked against any host until it arms one
87	## voltage [] | Voltage Definitions | None
88	{name?, nominal?, min?, max?, rename?, delete?: true} a voltage of the project's electrical settings, in volts: `nominal`, and the band a device may read within, `min` to `max` (10 per cent either way unless given). Without `name`, lists them. A voltage a distribution system names cannot be deleted; renamed, the systems follow
89	## distribution_system [] | Distribution Systems | None
90	{name?, phases?: 1|2|3, wires?, l_l?, l_n?, l_g?, ground?, rename?, delete?: true} a distribution system of the project's electrical settings. `wires` counts the line conductors and the neutral, not the protective one (3 phases: 3 or 4). `l_l`, `l_n` and `l_g` name the voltages between two lines, a line and the neutral, and a line and earth (at least one; `l_l` from 2 phases; with 3 phases `l_l` is about 1.73 times `l_n`), each a `voltage` of the project; "" takes one away. `ground` is the earthing: TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT or IT. A voltage the project lacks is refused, and the refusal lists the ones it has. Without `name`, lists them
91	## wire_type [] | Wire Types | None
92	{name?, material?: copper|aluminium, temperature?, insulation?, note?, sizes?: [{section, ampacity, label?}], rename?, delete?: true} a wire type of the project's electrical settings: a conductor's `material`, working `temperature` (°C) and `insulation`, and its table, `sizes`: the `section` of each row in mm² (smallest first, never less than the row before) and the `ampacity` it carries in amperes, with a `label` for how its standard names it (12 AWG). Giving `sizes` replaces the table. `note` says where the ampacities come from. Without `name`, lists them
93	## column ['CL'] | Column | Architecture > Column
94	{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`
95	## structural_column ['CL'] | Structural Column | None
96	{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one
97	## footing ['FI'] | Isolated Footing | None
98	{at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below
99	## beam ['BM'] | Beam | None
100	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°
101	## strip_footing ['FW'] | Wall Footing | None
102	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)
103	## pipe ['PI'] | Pipe | None
104	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")
105	## duct ['DU'] | Duct | None
106	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Supply air", "Exhaust")
107	## conduit ['CN'] | Conduit | None
108	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit
109	## cable_tray ['CT'] | Cable Tray | None
110	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep
111	## wire ['EW'] | Wire | None
112	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit
113	## down_conductor ['DC'] | Down Conductor | None
114	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to
115	## ground_conductor ['GC'] | Earthing Conductor | None
116	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)
117	## cabling ['CB'] | Cabling | None
118	{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to
119	## stair [] | Stair | Architecture > Stair
120	{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too
121
