## new [] | New | None
{name?, language?: en|pt|es|sv|cs|fr|nl} an empty project with Level 1 (0) and Level 2 (3000), named in its language (Nível 1, Nível 2 in Portuguese; Nivel 1, Nivel 2 in Spanish; Nivå 1, Nivå 2 in Swedish; Niveau 1, Niveau 2 in Dutch)
## open [] | Open | None
{path} a .bimcraft project
## highrise [] | Synthetic Highrise | None
{storeys?: 20} replace the project with an original 1–80 storey performance sample
## autosave [] | Autosave | None
{path} atomically write a recovery snapshot, keeping the project path and undo history
## recover [] | Recover Autosave | None
{path, project?} open and validate a recovery snapshot; Save targets `project`, or asks for Save As without it
## insert [] | Insert from File | None
{path, ids?: [id, …]} elements of another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) brought into this one: those `ids` names (their ids there), else all of them, and what they point at that this project hasn't (a level they stand on is this project's of the same name, where it has one). Each keeps its id unless this project has that id, and its GUID unless this project has that GUID: then it's a copy, with a GUID of its own (the same file inserted into itself is copied whole). What they point at among themselves follows them. A name or a number taken here gets ` 2`, ` 3`…; types, families, materials and parameters this project hasn't come by name, and so do the line styles (with their line patterns), fill patterns, filled region types and detail groups a detail line, a filled region or a group uses. Returns `ids` {there: here}, `copies`, `library`, `left_out`
## link ['LK'] | Link Model | Manage > Link Model
{path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees} another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited, as Revit's Link Revit: its walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and the rest of what it builds are drawn in the plans, sections and 3D views, halftone, and snapped to; nothing of it is selected, scheduled, checked or exported. It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`
## reload [] | Reload Links | None
{id?} read the file of the link `id`, or of every link, again: for a project that changed on disk. Returns `reloaded` (the names) and `failed` ({name, error})
## save [] | Save | None
{path?} .bimcraft saves the project (Save As with a path); .ifc exports IFC4; .glb exports the default 3D view's scene as glTF 2.0 (metres, y up, a node for each element named by its id, GUID and category in `extras`; returns `elements` and `triangles`); .svg or .png exports the lowest level's plan; .pdf prints every sheet, a page each
## undo [] | Undo | None
{count?} takes back the last `count` steps (1 by default)
## redo [] | Redo | None
{count?} does again the last `count` steps undone (1 by default)
## level ['LL'] | Level | Architecture > Level
{elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)
## grid ['GR'] | Grid | Architecture > Grid
{start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…
## point_cloud [] | Point Cloud | None
{path | cloud, name?, level?, at?: [x, y], offset?, angle?, units?, spacing?, origin?} brings in a laser scan (`path`: PTS, XYZ, PLY, LAS or E57 (each of its scans placed by its pose), or a list of the files of one scan's stations, brought in as one; `units` of its coordinates mm, cm, m (the default), in or ft; one point kept in each cube `spacing` mm wide) or places one the project holds again (`cloud`, its name), as an element: its middle on `at` (the origin) and its foot on the level, or with `origin: file` where its file's coordinates put it; `offset` raises its middle over the level, `angle` turns it. Returns its id, the scan's name, the points kept and read, and where its middle was in the file
## import_cad [] | Import CAD | None
{path | cad, name?, level?, view?, at?: [x, y], position?, units?, scale?, angle?, layers?, colors?, link?} brings in a DXF drawing (`path`: an ASCII DXF of any version, or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) or places one the project holds again (`cad`, its name), as an element in every plan of `level`, or with `view` (a plan) in that view only. `units` of the drawing: auto (the default: what its file says, else mm), mm, cm, m, in or ft; or `scale`, mm to each of its units. `position`: center (the default: the middle of the drawing on `at`, the origin unless given) or origin (its origin on `at`); `angle` turns it about `at`, degrees. `layers`: visible (the default: those its file has on and thawed), all, or a list of those to show. `colors`: preserve (the default), invert or black. `link: true` remembers the file, so `reload_cad` and opening the project read it again. Returns its id, the drawing's name, its unit, entities and layers, its extents in the model, how many entities lie far from the rest (they're left out of its extents) and what was left out, with `notes` on what a DWG's read left out
## cad_layers [] | CAD Layers | None
{id, hide?: [layer, …], show?: [layer, …], view?} a CAD import's layers, each with its colour and linetype and whether it's shown; `hide` and `show` change which it shows in every view, or with `view` in that view only (its Visibility/Graphics, by the drawing's name)
## reload_cad [] | Reload CAD | None
{cad} reads a linked CAD drawing's file again, so every import of it shows what the file holds now (opening the project does too). Returns whether it changed
## cad_query [] | Query | None
{id, at: [x, y], reach?} what of a CAD import lies nearest `at`, within `reach` mm (100 unless given): its kind, layer, colour, linetype and weight, as Revit's Query
## wall ['WA'] | Wall | Architecture > Wall
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them
## door ['DR'] | Door | Architecture > Door
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door
## window ['WN'] | Window | Architecture > Window
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)
## floor [] | Floor | Architecture > Floor
{boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline
## ceiling [] | Ceiling | Architecture > Ceiling
{point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it
## sketch [] | Sketch | None
{lines: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} solves a sketch without making anything, as Finish Edit Mode does: lines in any order, either way round, joined end to end (within 1 mm) into closed loops; a loop inside no other (or inside a hole) an outline, counter-clockwise, one inside an outline a hole in it, clockwise. Gives each region's `outline`, `holes` and `area_m2`, or every problem with the lines it's about (numbered from 0): ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line too: a polyline round a bow tie crosses itself), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight pieces its lines are drawn with (an arc, a circle or a curve is cut into chords, a circle into up to 8,193): past 200,000 of them, or when they lie so close together that telling which cross takes more than six million steps, it is refused at once. `sketch` on floor, ceiling, roof and shaft, and edit_boundary, take the same lines for one outline and its holes
## shaft [] | Shaft Opening | Architecture > Shaft
{boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`
## edit_boundary [] | Edit Boundary | None
{id, sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} redraws a floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's footprint's or a shaft's outline and its holes (a floor's or a ceiling's openings, a roof's courtyards; a shaft has none) as a sketch, all at once (see `sketch`); a roof's gable edges stay gables where the new footprint has the same edge. Without `sketch`, gives the outline and holes it has now, as the lines to edit. The outline must be simple, as `floor` says; a line that crosses itself is found as two that cross are
## edit_shape [] | Modify Sub Elements | None
{id, points?: [{at: [x,y], z, id?}, …], lines?: [{a: [x,y], b: [x,y], id?}, …], absolute?} gives a floor's top, or a flat roof's by footprint (its underside following), its shape anew, all at once: points `z` mm above (negative, below) where its top would be without them (with `absolute`, at that elevation), and split lines it folds along, between which it's flat triangles, merged where neighbours lie in one plane: falls to drains, ridges, valleys. Its outline's and openings' corners stay at 0 unless a point is there; a line's end that is no point and no corner becomes a point at the height the top has there. Sent back with its `id`, a point or a line keeps it. A shaped floor has no slope arrow, a shaped roof no `slope`. Without `points` or `lines`, gives the shape: its points and lines with their ids, its corners at their heights, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest (`top`, mm above zero)
## add_point [] | Add Point | None
{id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height
## add_split_line [] | Add Split Line | None
{id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now
## reset_shape [] | Reset Shape | None
{id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again
## falls [] | Falls | None
{id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest. Refused, saying why and where: a corner a drain can reach only over the outline or a ridge, or a plane that can't fall as asked to a drain
## mass ['MS'] | Mass | None
{boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`
## mass_floors ['MF'] | Mass Floors | None
{mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level
## wall_by_face ['WB'] | Wall by Face | None
{mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on
## floor_by_face ['FB'] | Floor by Face | None
{mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on
## roof_by_face ['RB'] | Roof by Face | None
{mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on
## update_by_face ['UF'] | Update to Face | None
{mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`
## show_mass ['MH'] | Show Mass | None
{view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's
## room ['RM'] | Room | Architecture > Room
{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen
## room_separator [] | Room Separator | None
{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids
## rebar [] | Rebar | None
{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule
## reinforce [] | Reinforce | None
{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes
## reinforcement_preset [] | Reinforcement Presets | None
{name?, kind?: beam|column|footing|floor, params?, rename?, delete?: true} a named set of the parameters `reinforce` takes for one kind of host (`params`: its `cover`, `grade`, `grade_stirrup`, `clearance` and what its kind takes, and not `host`), kept in the project; `reinforce` with `preset` takes it and lets what is given with it replace its own. Without `name`, lists them. It is not checked against any host until it arms one
## voltage [] | Voltage Definitions | None
{name?, nominal?, min?, max?, rename?, delete?: true} a voltage of the project's electrical settings, in volts: `nominal`, and the band a device may read within, `min` to `max` (10 per cent either way unless given). Without `name`, lists them. A voltage a distribution system names cannot be deleted; renamed, the systems follow
## distribution_system [] | Distribution Systems | None
{name?, phases?: 1|2|3, wires?, l_l?, l_n?, l_g?, ground?, rename?, delete?: true} a distribution system of the project's electrical settings. `wires` counts the line conductors and the neutral, not the protective one (3 phases: 3 or 4). `l_l`, `l_n` and `l_g` name the voltages between two lines, a line and the neutral, and a line and earth (at least one; `l_l` from 2 phases; with 3 phases `l_l` is about 1.73 times `l_n`), each a `voltage` of the project; "" takes one away. `ground` is the earthing: TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT or IT. A voltage the project lacks is refused, and the refusal lists the ones it has. Without `name`, lists them
## wire_type [] | Wire Types | None
{name?, material?: copper|aluminium, temperature?, insulation?, note?, sizes?: [{section, ampacity, label?}], rename?, delete?: true} a wire type of the project's electrical settings: a conductor's `material`, working `temperature` (°C) and `insulation`, and its table, `sizes`: the `section` of each row in mm² (smallest first, never less than the row before) and the `ampacity` it carries in amperes, with a `label` for how its standard names it (12 AWG). Giving `sizes` replaces the table. `note` says where the ampacities come from. Without `name`, lists them
## column ['CL'] | Column | Architecture > Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`
## structural_column ['CL'] | Structural Column | None
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one
## footing ['FI'] | Isolated Footing | None
{at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below
## beam ['BM'] | Beam | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°
## strip_footing ['FW'] | Wall Footing | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)
## pipe ['PI'] | Pipe | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")
## duct ['DU'] | Duct | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Supply air", "Exhaust")
## conduit ['CN'] | Conduit | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit
## cable_tray ['CT'] | Cable Tray | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep
## wire ['EW'] | Wire | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit
## down_conductor ['DC'] | Down Conductor | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to
## ground_conductor ['GC'] | Earthing Conductor | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)
## cabling ['CB'] | Cabling | None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to
## stair [] | Stair | Architecture > Stair
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too

1	## ramp [] | Ramp | Architecture > Ramp
2	{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level
3	## railing [] | Railing | Architecture > Railing

76	{ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids
77	## rotate ['RO'] | Rotate | None
78	{ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls
79	## mirror ['MM', 'DM'] | Mirror | None
80	{ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way
81	## corner ['TR'] | Trim/Extend to Corner | None
82	{ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep
83	## offset ['OF'] | Offset | None
84	{id, distance, toward: [x, y], copy?} a detail line drawn again `distance` mm beside itself on the side `toward` is, arcs round the same centres, an ellipse or a spline as a spline through points within 0.05 mm of the true offset (which Revit can't): a copy (the default), or with `copy` false moved
85	## trim_extend [] | Trim/Extend Single Element | None
86	{boundary, ids: [id, …], keep: [[x, y], …]} trims or extends each detail line of `ids` (lines and arcs) to where it meets `boundary` (a detail line, a wall's location line or a grid), keeping the part of each its `keep` point is on: Revit's Trim/Extend Single Element, and Multiple Elements with several
87	## split ['SL'] | Split | None
88	{id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`
89	## join_polyline ['PJ'] | Join into Polyline | None
90	{ids: [id, …]} joins detail lines of one view, lines, arcs and polylines that meet end to end, into one polyline in the first's line style (closed when they come round); the first keeps its id, the rest are deleted, and a dimension that measured one of the rest loses that reference (and is deleted, left with fewer than two): the reply's `notes` say which
91	## fillet ['FL'] | Fillet Arc | None
92	{ids: [a, b], radius} rounds the corner where two straight detail lines, or two straight walls, meet (or would, extended) with an arc of `radius` mm, in the first's line style or of the first's type: each is cut back to the arc
93	## vertex [] | Add/Delete Vertex | None
94	{id, at: [x, y], delete?} a detail line (a polyline, or a spline of either kind) with a vertex more where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points gains a control point and keeps its shape exactly), or with `delete` one fewer: the corner, control point or point passed through nearest `at`; `at` is within 100 mm of the line (of a vertex, to delete one), or it is refused
95	## convert_spline [] | Convert Spline | None
96	{id} a detail line that is a spline through points becomes the same curve by its control points, exactly; one by its control points becomes a spline through points within 0.05 mm of it
97	## explode ['EX'] | Explode Polyline | None
98	{id} takes a detail line that is a polyline apart into a line or an arc for each segment, in its view and style; the first keeps its id. Revit has no shortcut for it: EX is ours, PX being the Plumbing Fixture's on the desktop
99	## delete ['DE'] | Delete | None
100	{ids: [id,…]} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted

## ramp [] | Ramp | Architecture > Ramp
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level
## railing [] | Railing | Architecture > Railing
{host: a stair or a ramp, side?: left|right, type?} | {path: [[x,y],…], level?, base_offset?, type?} a railing along the stair's or the ramp's sides (both, or the one going up it on `side`), 50 mm in from its edges and climbing with it, going where it goes; or along `path`, `base_offset` mm above the level. Its type sets how high its rail stands over what it runs along, and how far apart its balusters are
## roof [] | Roof | Architecture > Roof
{level?, boundary?: [[x,y],…], courtyards?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], slope?, slopes?: [degrees, …], overhang?, gables?: [edge, …], gable?, offset?, extrusion?, openings?: [[[x,y],…],…], join?, type?} a roof on `level` (by default the one above the lowest), its base `offset` mm above it. Over `boundary` or else the walls of the level below, `overhang` mm (500) past their faces, round any `courtyards` (holes in it, inside it and apart, with eaves of their own; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it): flat at `slope` 0, else every edge sloping up at `slope` degrees (30), hips, valleys and ridges where the slopes meet, but the edges in `gables` (edge i runs from point i to the next, the courtyards' edges numbered on after the boundary's) left upright, gable ends; `gable` leaves a rectangle's short ends upright. `slopes`: a slope in degrees (up to 75) for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for an edge that takes `slope`; none, every edge does; the eaves stay level and an edge in `gables` stays upright whatever its slope. A `sketch` line may carry a `slope` for the edges along it. Or with `extrusion` {line: [[x,y],[x,y]], profile: [[along, up],…], from?, to}: its underside's profile in the upright plane through `line`, along it from its start and up from the base, swept square to it from `from` (0) to `to` mm to its left. `openings` are holes through it in plan; with `join`, a roof it runs into, it ends where it meets that one's top
## dormer [] | Dormer | Architecture > Dormer
{host, at: [x, y], width?, height?, slope?, window?, type?} a dormer on roof `host`, its front wall across the slope through `at`: walls of `type` `width` mm (1600) apart, standing on the roof and `height` mm (1200) tall at the front, under a gable roof of its own sloping `slope` degrees (30) that runs back into the host; the host open under it, and with `window` (a window type) a window in its front. Replies with its roof, walls and window
## dimension ['DI'] | Aligned Dimension | None
{refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 100 mm. It follows what it measures
## dimension_3d [] | Aligned Dimension in 3D | None
{refs: [ref, ref], at: [x, y, z], view?, type?} an aligned dimension in a 3D view (the default 3D view unless `view` names another, by name or id), kept by the view and drawn in it and on a sheet that holds it: how far apart its two references are, along a line through `at` moved square off them. A ref is {at: [x, y, z]}, a point of the model, or {at, edge: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]]}, a point on an edge, which it measures square to (from a point, to the edge's line; between two parallel edges, how far apart they are). `type` is a dimension type, the aligned one's unless told. On the desktop, Aligned Dimension (DI) in the 3D view runs it. Returns its id and its length
## text ['TX'] | Text | None
{text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's
## text_type [] | Text Types | None
{name?, font?, size?, bold?, italic?, underline?, width_factor?, color?, border?, border_offset?, border_pen?, like?, rename?, delete?: true} a text type of the project's: its `font`, any the system has, or one BIMCraft carries (IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, BIMCraft Lettering: single-stroke capitals); Arial, the default, letters on any system (where it isn't installed, Liberation Sans, Arimo, Helvetica or the like stands in, else IBM Plex Sans), and a font a file names that this system hasn't is stood in for likewise. Its capitals' height on paper (`size`, mm, 2.5 for a new one), bold, italic and underlined or not (a family's own bold and italic faces where it has them), `width_factor` (1: as the font draws it), its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), and whether a border is drawn round its notes, `border_offset` mm on paper out from their text (where a leader starts too; 1), in pen `border_pen` (0 to 16; 1). A new one starts as `like` says, or as 2.5mm Arial. A project starts with 2.5mm, 3.5mm and 5mm. `rename` renames it, its notes following; `delete` takes it away while no note is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type, the fonts this system has, and the font that letters each type here (`drawn_with`)
## dimension_constraint [] | Dimension Constraints | None
{id, equal?: bool, locked?: [segment, …]} an aligned or linear dimension's constraints, as Revit's EQ and padlocks: `equal` keeps its segments equal (what it measures to between its first and last moves to keep them so, its ends staying); `locked` lists the segments (counted from 0, west to east or south to north) kept at the lengths they have now. After any command, what a constrained dimension measures to moves with what the command moved, or the command is refused, saying which dimension can't be kept
## dimension_text [] | Dimension Text | None
{id, segment?, prefix?, suffix?, above?, below?, replace?} a dimension's text, as Revit's Dimension Text: what goes before and after its numbers, over and under them, or in place of them. With `segment` (its numbers counted from 0, west to east or south to north, as `labels` lists them), that one's own, over the dimension's where it says something; an empty text clears it, and a segment with none left goes back to the dimension's
## dimension_type [] | Dimension Types | None
{name?, like?, rename?, delete?: true, …values} a dimension type of the project's, as Revit's type parameters, lengths mm on paper. Graphics: `string` continuous|baseline|ordinate (Dimension String Type; baseline lines `baseline_spacing` apart, 7), `tick` diagonal|arrow|open_arrow|dot|none, `tick_size` (2), `line_pen` and `tick_pen` (0 to 16; 4 and 7), `color` ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b]), `line_extension` past the outer witness lines (0.8), `witness` gap_to_element|fixed (Witness Line Control), `witness_length` when fixed (5), `witness_gap` off what it measures (0.6), `witness_extension` past the dimension line (0.8), `centre_mark` on radial and diameter ones. Text: `font` (as text types take; Arial), `text_size` (2.5), `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `width_factor` (1), `text_offset` off the line (1), `background` opaque|transparent, `read` up_then_left|up_then_right (Read Convention), `units` (mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in; null for the project's) and `decimals` (0 to 6; null as the units show), `radius_symbol` (R), `diameter_symbol` (Ø), `equality_text` (EQ). A new one starts as `like` says, else as the default. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial` (aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in it) and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial` (radial and diameter ones). `rename` renames it, its dimensions following; `delete` takes it away while no dimension is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type
## spot ['EL'] | Spot Elevation | None
{at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot elevation: in a level's plan (the lowest by default), the height of the top of what stands on the level at `at` (or of `host`), following it; in a section or an elevation, of its point `at`, along and up
## spot_slope [] | Spot Slope | None
{at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot slope in a level's plan (the lowest by default): how steeply the top of the floor or roof at `at` (or `host`) falls there, %, an arrow pointing downhill; it follows the top. The reply gives `slope` and `toward`, the way down in plan (null on the level)
## tag ['TG'] | Tag by Category | None
{ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`
## section ['CR'] | Section | None
{start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything
## elevation [] | Elevation | None
{facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet
## sheet [] | Sheet | None
{number?, name?, size?: A0|A1|A2|A3|A4} a sheet of paper, landscape (A3 by default), with a title block; numbers run A101, A102…
## place [] | Place View | None
{sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`, 1 : 100 when it has none of its own; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default right of the views there, or in the middle); a view goes on one sheet. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed
## crop [] | Crop View | None
{view, region?: [[x, y], [x, y]] | null} crops a level's plan to the region's south-west and north-east corners (plan mm), or a section or an elevation to its bottom left and top right (along its line from its start, and up: its line then runs between them, and the notes in it stay put); null uncrops it; without a region, it crops to what the view shows now
## duplicate_view ['DP'] | Duplicate View | None
{view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it
## scale [] | View Scale | None
{view, scale?: 1 | … | 100000} a plan's, section's or elevation's scale, 1 : `scale`: the paper the view stands for, 1 mm of paper being `scale` mm of the model. Its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, tags, dimension ticks…) and its line weights (pens) are that paper's, so a screen shows them as the paper would at its zoom. Every view has one: 1 : 100 until it is given another, and null is refused. A view placed on a sheet takes it for the viewport's scale. Without `scale` it only says what the view has
## detail [] | Detail Level | None
{view, detail?: coarse | medium | fine} how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts: coarse, one poché and openings as their gaps; medium, compound layers with the lines between them and an opening's leaf, swing and glass; fine (the default), the layers' patterns and a floor's surface pattern too. Without `detail` it only says what the view has
## visual_style [] | Visual Style | None
{view?: "{3D}" | a 3D view's name or id, style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe} how a 3D view draws its surfaces: shaded (lit, in their materials' colours and textures, the default); hidden_line (paper-white with their edges, what a face hides staying hidden); wireframe (every edge, seen through the faces). Without `style` it only says what the view has; the default 3D view comes to be as it is first changed
## type [] | Edit Type | None
{category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)
## material [] | Materials | Manage > Materials
{name, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], transparency?: 0-100, cut?, surface?, texture?: {kind?, size?: [w, h], angle?, offset?: [x, y], path?, image?} | null, rename?, delete?: true} a material of the project's library, created or changed: its colour in shaded 3D views, its `transparency` there (percent of what lies behind it that shows through, 0 opaque; the starter Glass has 70), the pattern its cut shows in plans and sections (where a layer is wide enough to hold it), and the one its surfaces show at its size in the building (a floor's top in plan, a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan). Patterns: none, solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete, insulation, or the name of one of the project's fill patterns (see `fill_pattern`), kept while the material shows it and renamed with it. Its `texture` is what its surfaces look like in the 3D view, over its colour, a tile of it `size` mm across and up, turned `angle` degrees and moved `offset` mm: a pattern drawn in code, `kind` brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof, fabric, metal or insulation (at its natural size unless `size` says); or `image`, a picture: the PNG or JPEG file at `path`, taken into the project (up to 1024 px a side, 24 pictures), or one the project holds (`image`, its id from `inspect`); null takes the texture away. `rename` renames it, the layers using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no layer uses it. `inspect` lists the library and the pictures
## favorite [] | Favorites | Manage > Favorites
{action?: list|save|load|delete, kind?: material|family, name?, as?, replace?, path?} the user's favorites, kept in a file of their own (`path`; by default in their configuration folder) for every project to use: `save` the project's material or family `name` (a material with the picture its texture is made of, a family with the materials it is made of), under another name with `as`; `load` a favorite into the project, under another name with `as`, or over one it has already with `replace`; `delete` one from the favorites; `list` them (the default)
## paint ['PT'] | Paint | None
{id | ids, face?, material} paints a face of the elements with a material of the library, as Revit's Paint does: its colour and texture show in the 3D view over what their types are made of. `face`: a wall's `exterior` or `interior`, a floor's, roof's or ceiling's `top` or `bottom`, and `all` for a column, a component, a door, a window, a stair, a ramp or a railing; without it, every face the elements have. `material` null takes the paint off
## parameter [] | Project Parameters | Manage > Project Parameters
{name, kind?: text|number|length|yesno, categories?: [wall|floor|ceiling|roof|door|window|room|column|component|stair|ramp|railing|mass, …], rename?, delete?: true} a project parameter, as Revit's Manage > Project Parameters makes one: a value of its kind each element of its categories may have of its own, set with `modify {id, params: {name: value}}` (lengths in mm, yes or no as true or false). Off a category, that category's elements lose their values of it; deleted, every element does; renamed, they follow it. `inspect` lists them
## family [] | Load Family | Manage > Family Editor
{name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. {id, value, segment?} types a length into an aligned or a linear dimension's segment (the first unless told), as a click on its number does: what the segment ends at (its second reference, as the dimension runs west to east or south to north) moves along the dimension so the segment is `value` mm; a locked segment is locked at it, and the other locks hold, or it is refused. {id} a detail line that is a spline through points becomes the same curve by its control points, exactly; one by its control points becomes a spline through points within 0.05 mm of it

{id} takes a detail line that is a polyline apart into a line or an arc for each segment, in its view and style; the first keeps its id. Revit has no shortcut for it: EX is ours, PX being the Plumbing Fixture's on the desktop
