55	## graphics [] | Visibility/Graphics | None
56	{view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or {3D} (the lowest level's plan unless given), hide?: [category, …], show?: […], hide_elements?: [id, …], show_elements?: […], categories?: {category: override | null, …}, elements?: {id: override | null, …}, filters?: [{filter, hidden?, projection?, cut?, halftone?, transparency?}, …], phase?: name | null, phase_filter?: name | null, options?: {set: option | null, …}, layers?: {drawing: [layer, …] | null, …}, template?: name | null, background_grid?: {visible?, main?: {enabled?, color?: [r,g,b], pen?: 0..16}, sub?: {enabled?, color?, pen?}, spacing?: [X,Y] (mm), divisions?: [X,Y] (1..1000), rotation?: degrees (-360..360)} | null, reset?: true} what a view hides and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does; with none of those, the view's settings as they are. A category hidden (walls, floors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels…, in any case, singular or plural) leaves all its elements out of that view, and `hide_elements` the elements given. In a 3D view rooms are hidden unless shown (`show: [rooms]`), every new 3D view so; shown, each is a see-through solid. Subcategories are hidden and shown as categories are, and go with their category: under rooms, `roomreference` (the cross at each room's point, hidden unless shown, as Revit's Rooms > Reference) and `roomseparator` (room separation lines). An override is {hidden?, projection?: style, cut?: style, halftone?, transparency?}, a style {color?, weight? (a pen, 0 to 16: 0 a hairline, the thinnest line the screen or printer draws at any scale; 1 to 16 widths on paper from 0.10 to 4 mm, 4 being 0.18 mm and 10 0.35 mm, a cut wall's outline), dash? (solid, dashed, dotted), fill?, foreground?, background?}, a colour [r, g, b] or "#rrggbb". Foreground and background override independent pattern layers: {pattern: a fill pattern's name | null, color?: [r,g,b]}; a null pattern hides that layer; a null foreground or background restores inheritance. They draw in plans, ceiling plans, section cuts and filled regions, using drafting patterns at paper scale and model patterns at model size. Projection is what a plan sees below its cut plane, a section beyond its line and the annotation; cut is what the view cuts; `fill` is the cut's poché, or a 3D view's surface; in a 3D view, and in what a section sees beyond its line, a projection's `color` is the colour of the edges (weight and dash draw lines, and those are vectors). Halftone draws it halfway to the paper; transparency (percent) sees through it in a 3D view. Halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can lighten what its category doesn't, not take its category's away. Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the phase the view shows (the project's last unless it says) and `phase_filter` how it shows each status of what's in it (see `phase`); `options` chooses the design option it shows of a set (the set's primary unless it says; see `option`); `layers` the layers of each CAD drawing it hides, by the drawing's name (null shows them all again)
57	## section_box [] | Section Box | None
58	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again
59	## perspective [] | Perspective | None
60	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands
61	## graphic_display_options ['GD'] | Graphic Display Options | None
62	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), edges?: true | false, silhouette?: px, ambient_shadows?: true | false} how a 3D view draws its edges and shadows, as Revit's Graphic Display Options: `edges`, the lines where its surfaces meet in Shaded (on unless turned off; Hidden Line always draws them); `silhouette`, an outline that many pixels wide (a whole number, 0 to 10; 0, the default, for none) round what stands in front of what is further off or of nothing; `ambient_shadows`, soft shadows where faces meet inside a corner (off unless turned on). What is left out stays as it was; with none of them it only says what the view has
63	## camera [] | Camera | None
64	{eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in
65	## work_plane [] | Work Plane | None
66	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. Says the plane: a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level
67	## filter [] | View Filter | None
68	{name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. A view applies it with `graphics {filters}`, hiding what it picks out or drawing it another way. Gone, views stop applying it. Replies with the filter and the ids it picks out; `name` alone reads one
69	## template [] | View Template | None
70	{name, from?: a level's, section's, elevation's or 3D view's name or id, like?: another template's name, kind?: plan | section | 3d | null, rename?, controls?: [categories, filters, range, phase, options, scale, detail, style, background_grid], view_range?: {top?, cut?, bottom?, depth?}, phase?, phase_filter?, options?, scale?: 1 | … | 100000, detail?: coarse | medium | fine, visual_style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe, background_grid?: grid settings as in graphics, hide?, show?, categories?, filters?, reset?, delete?: true} a view template, as Revit's: settings under a name for views to follow with `graphics {template}`. `kind` is the views it is for (plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; null, any), which `from` sets; `like` makes a new one a copy of another (Duplicate); `rename` names it anew, and its views follow it under that name. `from` takes a view's categories (hidden and overridden), filters and, a plan's, view range, its phase and phase filter, its design options, its scale, detail level and visual style; `controls` is what views following it get from it (all nine unless it says) and cannot change for themselves: its categories, its filters, a plan's view range, its phase with its phase filter, its design options, its scale (`scale` command), its detail level (`detail`), its visual style (`visual_style`). `hide`, `show`, `categories`, `filters`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `background_grid` and `reset` change it as they change a view; `view_range` merges into its range. Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one
71	## phase [] | Phasing | Manage > Phasing
72	{name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides
73	## phase_filter [] | Phase Filter | Manage > Phasing
74	{name, new?, existing?, demolished?, temporary?, delete?} a phase filter: how a view shows each status of what's in its phase, each `by-category` (as its category and the view's overrides say), `overridden` (as the project's overrides for that status say) or `not-displayed`. A project has Show All, Show Complete, Show New, Show Previous + Demolished and Show Previous + New; any may change. A new one starts by category throughout. One in use by a view or a template can't be deleted. Replies with the filter
75	## option [] | Design Options | Manage > Design Options
76	{set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)
77	## measure ['ME'] | Measure | None
78	{from: [x, y], to: [x, y]} what a ruler laid between two points reads (mm): its `length`, its parts `dx` and `dy`, and its `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise; it changes nothing
79	## circuit [] | Size a Circuit | None
80	{load, apparent?, demand?, power_factor?, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, system?: 127/220|220/380|230/400, use?: lighting|power, length?, method?, insulation?: pvc|epr, conductor?: flexible|rigid, ambient?, grouped?, bundle?, spacing?, soil?, section?, breaker?, drop_limit?, reduced_neutral?} one electrical circuit sized as NBR 5410:2004 asks, for copper: `load` in W (or VA with `apparent`), `demand` (0 to 1, 1) and `power_factor` (over 0 to 1, 1; a first value, not a claim about the load), `phases` (FN one phase and neutral, the default; FF; 3F; 3FN balanced), the voltage `system` (127/220), `use` (power: 2.5 mm² at least; lighting 1.5), `length` to the farthest load (mm; none: no drop is checked), the installation `method` of Tabela 33 (7: a conduit in masonry; also 1 to 8, 11, 11A, 61, 61A), `insulation` (pvc 70 °C, or epr 90 °C), `conductor` (flexible, the larger resistance; or rigid), `ambient` °C (30 in air, 20 in soil), `grouped` circuits in the conduit (this one included), `bundle` (method 11 cables bundled), `spacing` between buried conduits (mm) and `soil` resistivity (K·m/W), and a `section` (mm²) and `breaker` (A) already chosen, which are never made smaller. Replies with the design current, the section and breaker that give I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) with the drop within `drop_limit` (4 %), the current the section carries, the drop, the conductors (phases, neutral, protective), the factors, and what the chosen section and breaker give. It changes nothing; aluminium, trays, several layers, short circuit and harmonics are not checked. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it
81	## conduit_fill [] | Conduit Fill | None
82	{section, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, circuits?, reduced_neutral?, family?, size?} the fill of a conduit as NBR 5410 asks, for the conductors of a circuit (its phases, neutral and protective conductor, of `section` mm²) times `circuits` in the same conduit (1): their cross-sections by outside diameter over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two, 40 % for three or more. `family` (pvc-thread, pvc-solder, steel-heavy, steel-rir; pvc-thread) and `size` (its mark, e.g. 3/4"; none: the smallest that fits). The dimensions are the makers' own from their catalogues, each family naming maker, document, page and address; the inside diameter is the outside less twice the wall. The data covers the flexible 750 V PVC cable of 0.5 to 240 mm² only: there is no `insulation` key, and a section above 240 mm² is `pending`, never guessed. `sections_mm2` lists the conductors of one circuit (`circuits` of them are in the conduit). Cable trays are not sized. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
83	## drain_size [] | Size a Sanitary Drain | None
84	{units?, fixtures?: {wc?, lav?, sink?, shower?, laundry?}, role?: branch|main|stack, slope?, floors?, min_dn?} the DN of a sanitary drain as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) it carries: `units`, or `fixtures` counted (Tabela 3: a water closet 6 UHC and DN 100, a lavatory 1 and 40, a sink 3 and 50, a shower 2 and 40, a laundry tub 3 and 40; the drain is never smaller than the fixtures' own). `role`: a `branch` (ramal de esgoto, Tabela 5, the default), a `main` (subcoletor or coletor predial, Tabela 7 by `slope`, a fraction, 0.01 by default; DN 100 at least) or a `stack` (tubo de queda, Tabela 6 by the building's `floors`, up to three or more). `min_dn` is the largest drain flowing into it. Replies with the `dn`, what it carries (`capacity`) and the `minimum_dn` the fixtures ask. A blank in the standard's table means not allowed: DN 100 and 150 carry nothing in a building drain at 0.5 %, and a branch or a building drain never borrows the other's table. For a `main` every fixture given counts, where item 5.1.4.2 counts only the largest fixture of each bathroom in a residential building: pass `units` already reduced to follow it. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
85	## vent_size [] | Size a Sanitary Vent | None
86	{units, wc?, stack_dn?, length?, trap_dn?} the DN of a sanitary vent as NBR 8160 asks, by the units (UHC) of what it vents: a branch vent (ramal de ventilação, Tabela 8; `wc` says a water closet is in the group), or, with `stack_dn` (the DN of the stack or drain served) and `length` (mm, from its foot to its open end), a vent stack or header (Tabela 2). `trap_dn` adds the longest run from a trap of that DN to its vent (Tabela 1). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
87	## hydrant_size [] | Size Hydrants | None
88	{column?: 1-5, area?, type?: 1|2|3|4-40|4-65|5, hydrants?, inside?, nominal?, material?: steel|steel-wet|copper|pvc|pex, length?, rise?} hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks. With `column` (of Tabela 3, by the occupation) and `area` (m², built) it replies the system type and the fire reserve (m³). With `type` (Tabela 2; 4 comes as 4-40 or 4-65 by its nozzle) it replies the design flow, that of the two most unfavourable jets (`hydrants`, 2 by default), and the head at the nozzle; with `inside` (mm) it also replies the speed (5 m/s at most), the Hazen-Williams head loss over `length` (m) of the `material` (Tabela 1: `steel` is black steel in a dry system, C 100, the lowest steel row and the default, `steel-wet` is galvanised or wet, C 120), the head needed at the start of the pipe with its `rise` (mm, up) and, with `nominal` (mm), whether the pipe is big enough (DN 65; DN 50 for types 1 and 2). `length` and `rise` are in millimetres. `need_mca` is the nozzle head + the head loss of the straight pipe + the rise: it leaves out the hose, the fittings and the pressure at the source (`need_covers` says so), and `ok` is only the nozzle head within 100 mca, the speed and the pipe's size (`ok_covers`), not a verdict on the design. A `type` that contradicts `column` and `area` is an error. Notes 1 and 2 of Tabela 3 (a system one type lower in some cases) are not applied. `region` is SP, the only one: this is the São Paulo rule, and no other state's. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
89	## load_points [] | Residential Load Points | None
90	{rooms?: [{name, area, perimeter, kind?: bath|kitchen|service|dry|veranda|other, points?}], alternative?} the lighting and the general-use outlets (TUG) of a dwelling's rooms as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks. The rooms are `rooms` (`area` in m², `perimeter` in millimetres, `points` the outlets the room has, the least it needs when absent) or, without it, the rooms of the model, measured inside the walls' finish. A room's kind is known by its name (Portuguese or English: banheiro, cozinha, copa, área de serviço, lavanderia, sala, dormitório, varanda…) unless `kind` gives it; a name that says none is `other`. Lighting: 1 ceiling point of 100 VA up to 6 m² and 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above. Outlets: a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area, laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room, bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and one for each 5 m above. Power: in a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry 600 VA for each of the first 3 points and 100 VA for the others; elsewhere 100 VA a point; on the points a room has. Where those rooms have more than 6 points together `alternative: true` takes 600 VA for the first 2 of each (`alternative_possible` says when). A kitchen or pantry also needs 2 outlets over the sink's counter (`counter_outlets`). Not applied: the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, the placement of the outlets and the TUE (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
91	## water_size [] | Size Cold Water Pipes | None
92	{fixtures?: {wc, lav, sink, shower, laundry: count}, flow?, method?: weights|sum, dn?, length?, fittings?: {elbow90, elbow45, tee_through, tee_side, gate, globe, check: count}, pressure?, rise?} a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/s), or the design flow of the `fixtures` by the `method` the project chooses: weights (the empirical method, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, never more than the fixtures' own flows; the default) or sum (every fixture at once). The fixture flows and weights are Tigre's (Manual Técnico, page 198), not the standard's; `wc` is the WC with a flush tank only (a flush-valve WC is not in the table here). Without `dn` it replies the smallest DN chosen by speed alone (3 m/s at most; the pressure is not used to choose it); with `dn`, whether that pipe keeps the speed. The head loss is Darcy-Weisbach (Colebrook, PVC at 20 °C) over `length` (mm) plus the equivalent length of the `fittings`; with `pressure` (kPa, dynamic, upstream) and `rise` (mm, up) it replies the pressure left at the end, 10 kPa at least at a point of use, and `ok` covers both; without `pressure` `ok` is the speed alone (`ok_covers` says which). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
93	## storm_size [] | Size a Storm Drain | None
94	{kind: downpipe|horizontal, area?, rainfall?, flow?, outlet?: edge|funnel, gutter?, length?, slope?, inside?} a storm drain as NBR 10844 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/min), or the rain on `area` (m², as the standard counts a roof) at `rainfall` (mm/h; 150 by default, which the standard allows for up to 100 m² only: above that `rainfall` is required): Q = I·A/60. A `downpipe` (condutor vertical) takes the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses by Q, the water depth in the gutter `gutter` (50 to 100 mm), its `length` (mm, 0.3 m or more) and the gutter's `outlet` (edge: sharp-edged, the default; funnel); 70 mm inside at least. A `horizontal` drain takes Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, PVC only, from the standard's Table 2) at its `slope` (a fraction, 0.005 at least): the inner diameter it needs, and with `inside` (mm) whether that pipe carries the flow. Off the abacuses (more than 150 mm inside) nothing is read. A key that does not apply to the `kind`, or `flow` together with `area`, is an error. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
95	## library [] | Library | None
96	{kind?, name?} the project's library with its ids and GUIDs, as elements have them: each type (`kind` `type:wall`, `type:door`, `type:beam`…), material, picture, family, parameter, view filter and template (`view-filter`, `view-template`), phase, phase filter, design option set and design option (`option-set`, `design-option`, named `set: option`), family type and family parameter (`family-type`, `family-parameter`, named `family: name`); and `parts`, what entries hold that has its own id and GUID: each type's layers and each family's forms and symbols (`kind` `layer`, `form`, `symbol`; `name` the type's or the family's). Wherever a command takes an entry by name, its GUID does too
97	## select_by_id [] | Select by ID | Manage > Select by ID
98	{text} the elements a list names, each by its id, its GUID (dashes and braces or not) or its IFC GlobalId, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons or lines: `ids` found, each once in the order named, `missing` (what named none), and `plan` and `extent` ([[x, y], [x, y]] mm), the level's plan that shows them and where; it selects nothing itself, a front end does
99	## ids_of [] | IDs of Selection | Manage > IDs of Selection
100	{ids: [id or GUID, …]} what names each element: its `id`, its `guid`, its `ifc` GlobalId, its `category` and its `name` (or type, number, mark)
101	## filter_selection [] | Filter | None
102	{ids: [id or GUID, …], by?, keep?: [value, …]} Revit's Filter on a selection: `groups` [{value, count, ids}, …], the values `by` takes among the elements (by default `Category`, whose values are categories' keys: wall, door, detail_line…; else a parameter as `fields` lists them, values as schedules show them, `""` for none), and `fields`, the parameters every one of them has, to filter by. With `keep`, `ids`: those holding one of its values, the selection to keep; it selects nothing itself, a front end does
103	## elements [] | Elements | None
104	{category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do
105

## line_pattern [] | Line Patterns | None
{name?, segments?: [{dash: mm} | {space: mm} | "dot" | {dot_length: mm} | {offset: {length, count, distance}} | {wave: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {zigzag: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {text: {length, size, text}}, …], rename?, delete?: true} a line pattern of the project's: 1–32 freely ordered graphic segments, each 0.05–100 mm long on paper, so it reads the same at any scale. Offsets have 2–9 lines spaced symmetrically; frequency is cycles per segment, 0.1–100; amplitude and spacing are mm. Text uses bundled IBM Plex Sans, size is maximum capital height (shrinks to fit length), 1–256 single-line characters, following the curve. All graphics preserve the centerline. A project starts with Dash, Long Dash, Dot, Dash Dot, Hidden and Centre; Solid is a line with none. `rename` renames it, the line styles using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no style uses it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern
## line_style [] | Line Styles | Manage > Line Styles
{name?, pen?, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], pattern?: name | "Solid", rename?, delete?: true} a line style of the project's, as Revit's: the pen (0, a hairline, to 16) its lines draw in, their colour (black unless told) and their line pattern. A new one needs `pen`; one changed keeps what it isn't given. A project starts with Hairline, Thin Lines, Medium Lines, Wide Lines, Hidden Lines, Centre Lines and Overhead Lines. `rename` renames it, the lines drawn in it following; `delete` takes it away, while no line is drawn in it. Without `name`, it lists every style
## fill_pattern [] | Fill Patterns | Manage > Fill Patterns
{name?, target?: drafting|model, lines?: [{angle, spacing, origin?: [x, y], shift?, dashes?: [mm, -mm, …]}, …], drawn?: scale | null, rename?, delete?: true} a fill pattern of the project's, as Revit's (and a PAT file's): families of parallel lines, each at `angle` degrees through `origin`, its lines `spacing` apart and each `shift` along from the last, whole or dashed (`dashes`: a dash's length, a space's as a negative one, 0 a dot); no lines, it fills solid. A drafting pattern's lengths are mm on paper, the same at any scale; a model pattern's mm in the building. A project starts with Solid fill, Diagonal Up and Down, Crosshatch, Diagonal Crosshatch, Horizontal, Vertical, Sand, Brick 225 x 75 and Tile 300. `rename` renames it, the region types filling with it following; `delete` takes it away while no type uses it. `drawn` is the scale (1 : n, its n) of the view one made of lines (`make_fill_pattern`) was drawn in: such a one given a new `target` and no `lines` is rescaled, a drafting one being the drawing on paper at that scale; null forgets it. {load, apparent?, demand?, power_factor?, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, system?: 127/220|220/380|230/400, use?: lighting|power, length?, method?, insulation?: pvc|epr, conductor?: flexible|rigid, ambient?, grouped?, bundle?, spacing?, soil?, section?, breaker?, drop_limit?, reduced_neutral?} one electrical circuit sized as NBR 5410:2004 asks, for copper: `load` in W (or VA with `apparent`), `demand` (0 to 1, 1) and `power_factor` (over 0 to 1, 1; a first value, not a claim about the load), `phases` (FN one phase and neutral, the default; FF; 3F; 3FN balanced), the voltage `system` (127/220), `use` (power: 2.5 mm² at least; lighting 1.5), `length` to the farthest load (mm; none: no drop is checked), the installation `method` of Tabela 33 (7: a conduit in masonry; also 1 to 8, 11, 11A, 61, 61A), `insulation` (pvc 70 °C, or epr 90 °C), `conductor` (flexible, the larger resistance; or rigid), `ambient` °C (30 in air, 20 in soil), `grouped` circuits in the conduit (this one included), `bundle` (method 11 cables bundled), `spacing` between buried conduits (mm) and `soil` resistivity (K·m/W), and a `section` (mm²) and `breaker` (A) already chosen, which are never made smaller. Replies with the design current, the section and breaker that give I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) with the drop within `drop_limit` (4 %), the current the section carries, the drop, the conductors (phases, neutral, protective), the factors, and what the chosen section and breaker give. It changes nothing; aluminium, trays, several layers, short circuit and harmonics are not checked. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it
## conduit_fill [] | Conduit Fill | None
{section, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, circuits?, reduced_neutral?, family?, size?} the fill of a conduit as NBR 5410 asks, for the conductors of a circuit (its phases, neutral and protective conductor, of `section` mm²) times `circuits` in the same conduit (1): their cross-sections by outside diameter over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two, 40 % for three or more. `family` (pvc-thread, pvc-solder, steel-heavy, steel-rir; pvc-thread) and `size` (its mark, e.g. 3/4"; none: the smallest that fits). The dimensions are the makers' own from their catalogues, each family naming maker, document, page and address; the inside diameter is the outside less twice the wall. The data covers the flexible 750 V PVC cable of 0.5 to 240 mm² only: there is no `insulation` key, and a section above 240 mm² is `pending`, never guessed. `sections_mm2` lists the conductors of one circuit (`circuits` of them are in the conduit). Cable trays are not sized. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
## drain_size [] | Size a Sanitary Drain | None
{units?, fixtures?: {wc?, lav?, sink?, shower?, laundry?}, role?: branch|main|stack, slope?, floors?, min_dn?} the DN of a sanitary drain as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) it carries: `units`, or `fixtures` counted (Tabela 3: a water closet 6 UHC and DN 100, a lavatory 1 and 40, a sink 3 and 50, a shower 2 and 40, a laundry tub 3 and 40; the drain is never smaller than the fixtures' own). `role`: a `branch` (ramal de esgoto, Tabela 5, the default), a `main` (subcoletor or coletor predial, Tabela 7 by `slope`, a fraction, 0.01 by default; DN 100 at least) or a `stack` (tubo de queda, Tabela 6 by the building's `floors`, up to three or more). `min_dn` is the largest drain flowing into it. Replies with the `dn`, what it carries (`capacity`) and the `minimum_dn` the fixtures ask. A blank in the standard's table means not allowed: DN 100 and 150 carry nothing in a building drain at 0.5 %, and a branch or a building drain never borrows the other's table. For a `main` every fixture given counts, where item 5.1.4.2 counts only the largest fixture of each bathroom in a residential building: pass `units` already reduced to follow it. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
## vent_size [] | Size a Sanitary Vent | None
{units, wc?, stack_dn?, length?, trap_dn?} the DN of a sanitary vent as NBR 8160 asks, by the units (UHC) of what it vents: a branch vent (ramal de ventilação, Tabela 8; `wc` says a water closet is in the group), or, with `stack_dn` (the DN of the stack or drain served) and `length` (mm, from its foot to its open end), a vent stack or header (Tabela 2). `trap_dn` adds the longest run from a trap of that DN to its vent (Tabela 1). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
## hydrant_size [] | Size Hydrants | None
{column?: 1-5, area?, type?: 1|2|3|4-40|4-65|5, hydrants?, inside?, nominal?, material?: steel|steel-wet|copper|pvc|pex, length?, rise?} hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks. With `column` (of Tabela 3, by the occupation) and `area` (m², built) it replies the system type and the fire reserve (m³). With `type` (Tabela 2; 4 comes as 4-40 or 4-65 by its nozzle) it replies the design flow, that of the two most unfavourable jets (`hydrants`, 2 by default), and the head at the nozzle; with `inside` (mm) it also replies the speed (5 m/s at most), the Hazen-Williams head loss over `length` (m) of the `material` (Tabela 1: `steel` is black steel in a dry system, C 100, the lowest steel row and the default, `steel-wet` is galvanised or wet, C 120), the head needed at the start of the pipe with its `rise` (mm, up) and, with `nominal` (mm), whether the pipe is big enough (DN 65; DN 50 for types 1 and 2). `length` and `rise` are in millimetres. `need_mca` is the nozzle head + the head loss of the straight pipe + the rise: it leaves out the hose, the fittings and the pressure at the source (`need_covers` says so), and `ok` is only the nozzle head within 100 mca, the speed and the pipe's size (`ok_covers`), not a verdict on the design. A `type` that contradicts `column` and `area` is an error. Notes 1 and 2 of Tabela 3 (a system one type lower in some cases) are not applied. `region` is SP, the only one: this is the São Paulo rule, and no other state's. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
## load_points [] | Residential Load Points | None
{rooms?: [{name, area, perimeter, kind?: bath|kitchen|service|dry|veranda|other, points?}], alternative?} the lighting and the general-use outlets (TUG) of a dwelling's rooms as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks. The rooms are `rooms` (`area` in m², `perimeter` in millimetres, `points` the outlets the room has, the least it needs when absent) or, without it, the rooms of the model, measured inside the walls' finish. A room's kind is known by its name (Portuguese or English: banheiro, cozinha, copa, área de serviço, lavanderia, sala, dormitório, varanda…) unless `kind` gives it; a name that says none is `other`. Lighting: 1 ceiling point of 100 VA up to 6 m² and 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above. Outlets: a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area, laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room, bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and one for each 5 m above. Power: in a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry 600 VA for each of the first 3 points and 100 VA for the others; elsewhere 100 VA a point; on the points a room has. Where those rooms have more than 6 points together `alternative: true` takes 600 VA for the first 2 of each (`alternative_possible` says when). A kitchen or pantry also needs 2 outlets over the sink's counter (`counter_outlets`). Not applied: the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, the placement of the outlets and the TUE (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
## water_size [] | Size Cold Water Pipes | None
{fixtures?: {wc, lav, sink, shower, laundry: count}, flow?, method?: weights|sum, dn?, length?, fittings?: {elbow90, elbow45, tee_through, tee_side, gate, globe, check: count}, pressure?, rise?} a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/s), or the design flow of the `fixtures` by the `method` the project chooses: weights (the empirical method, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, never more than the fixtures' own flows; the default) or sum (every fixture at once). The fixture flows and weights are Tigre's (Manual Técnico, page 198), not the standard's; `wc` is the WC with a flush tank only (a flush-valve WC is not in the table here). Without `dn` it replies the smallest DN chosen by speed alone (3 m/s at most; the pressure is not used to choose it); with `dn`, whether that pipe keeps the speed. The head loss is Darcy-Weisbach (Colebrook, PVC at 20 °C) over `length` (mm) plus the equivalent length of the `fittings`; with `pressure` (kPa, dynamic, upstream) and `rise` (mm, up) it replies the pressure left at the end, 10 kPa at least at a point of use, and `ok` covers both; without `pressure` `ok` is the speed alone (`ok_covers` says which). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
## storm_size [] | Size a Storm Drain | None
{kind: downpipe|horizontal, area?, rainfall?, flow?, outlet?: edge|funnel, gutter?, length?, slope?, inside?} a storm drain as NBR 10844 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/min), or the rain on `area` (m², as the standard counts a roof) at `rainfall` (mm/h; 150 by default, which the standard allows for up to 100 m² only: above that `rainfall` is required): Q = I·A/60. A `downpipe` (condutor vertical) takes the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses by Q, the water depth in the gutter `gutter` (50 to 100 mm), its `length` (mm, 0.3 m or more) and the gutter's `outlet` (edge: sharp-edged, the default; funnel); 70 mm inside at least. A `horizontal` drain takes Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, PVC only, from the standard's Table 2) at its `slope` (a fraction, 0.005 at least): the inner diameter it needs, and with `inside` (mm) whether that pipe carries the flow. Off the abacuses (more than 150 mm inside) nothing is read. A key that does not apply to the `kind`, or `flow` together with `area`, is an error. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing
## library [] | Library | None
{kind?, name?} the project's library with its ids and GUIDs, as elements have them: each type (`kind` `type:wall`, `type:door`, `type:beam`…), material, picture, family, parameter, view filter and template (`view-filter`, `view-template`), phase, phase filter, design option set and design option (`option-set`, `design-option`, named `set: option`), family type and family parameter (`family-type`, `family-parameter`, named `family: name`); and `parts`, what entries hold that has its own id and GUID: each type's layers and each family's forms and symbols (`kind` `layer`, `form`, `symbol`; `name` the type's or the family's). Wherever a command takes an entry by name, its GUID does too
## select_by_id [] | Select by ID | Manage > Select by ID
{text} the elements a list names, each by its id, its GUID (dashes and braces or not) or its IFC GlobalId, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons or lines: `ids` found, each once in the order named, `missing` (what named none), and `plan` and `extent` ([[x, y], [x, y]] mm), the level's plan that shows them and where; it selects nothing itself, a front end does
## ids_of [] | IDs of Selection | Manage > IDs of Selection
{ids: [id or GUID, …]} what names each element: its `id`, its `guid`, its `ifc` GlobalId, its `category` and its `name` (or type, number, mark)
## filter_selection [] | Filter | None
{ids: [id or GUID, …], by?, keep?: [value, …]} Revit's Filter on a selection: `groups` [{value, count, ids}, …], the values `by` takes among the elements (by default `Category`, whose values are categories' keys: wall, door, detail_line…; else a parameter as `fields` lists them, values as schedules show them, `""` for none), and `fields`, the parameters every one of them has, to filter by. With `keep`, `ids`: those holding one of its values, the selection to keep; it selects nothing itself, a front end does
## elements [] | Elements | None
{category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do

mkdir -p /tmp/tpl && cd /tmp/tpl && for l in en pt es sv cs fr nl de it; do /workspace/executable run --cmd "new {\"language\": \"$l\"}" --save $l.bimcraft > /dev/null; done; /workspace/executable run --save default.bimcraft >/dev/null; python3 /tmp/tools/norm.py default.bimcraft > d.norm; python3 /tmp/tools/norm.py en.bimcraft > e.norm; diff d.norm e.norm && echo "default==en"; cat > /tmp/tools/mktpl.py <<'EOF'
import json, re, sys
langs = ['en','pt','es','sv','cs','fr','nl','de','it']
out = ['//! The default contents of a new project in each language: what `new` makes, with',
       '//! `@G<n>` standing for a GUID made fresh for each project.',
       '']
for l in langs:
    s = open(f'/tmp/tpl/{l}.bimcraft').read()
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": 0', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m:
            m[g] = '@G%d' % len(m)
        return m[g]
